item.title: When Ethylene Meets Sulfur: Direct Synthesis of Minimal Ethylene-Sulfur Copolymers
item.description: In inverse vulcanization chemistry, research has predominantly focused on multifunctional unsaturated comonomers to stabilize sulfur-rich structures, whereas the direct copolymerization of elemental sulfur with simple olefins has remained comparatively unexplored. Extending this concept to the simplest olefin, we report Minimal Ethylene-Sulfur Copolymers (MinESC), synthesized through the direct reaction of gaseous ethylene with elemental sulfur via a base-mediated inverse vulcanization approach under mild conditions. These materials are viscoelastic fluids of tunable viscosity reaching exceptionally high values. They exhibit a peculiar sheet-like morphology, polar surfaces, elevated electrical conductivity, and high permittivity, and can be reprocessed into predominantly elastic structures following thermal treatment. Our approach provides a straightforward route to a distinct class of sulfurethylene-derived functional materials and demonstrates that inverse vulcanization chemistry can be extended to the simplest olefin under industrially relevant pressures and temperatures.

item.title: Photocatalytic CO2 Conversion Driven by UV Light Above 300 nm Using Ammonia as an Electron Donor
item.description: Efficient utilisation of solar UV light (λ > 300 nm) is essential for practical photocatalytic CO2 conversion. However, in conventional systems using water as an electron donor, slow water oxidation kinetics present a critical bottleneck that severely limits the CO production rate. Here, we demonstrate an efficient CO2 conversion system that overcomes this kinetic limitation by employing ammonia as an alternative electron donor over Mg-doped SrTiO3 loaded with Ag and Fe as dualcocatalysts (Ag–Fe/Mg–SrTiO3). Under UV irradiation (λ > 300 nm), the optimised photocatalyst achieved a remarkable CO produc on rate exceeding 200 μmol h−1. Mechanistic investigations revealed that the Fe cocatalyst played a crucial role in promoting ammonia oxidation, facilitating the rapid consumption of photogenerated holes, and significantly enhancing CO2 conversion activity. Furthermore, nitrite (NO2−) was successfully quantified as the primary oxidation product of ammonia, yielding a calculated e−/h+ balance of approximately 1.2, validating the stoichiometric relationship of the reaction. This study offers a promising strategy for simultaneously achieving the upcycling of CO2 and effective utilisation of ammonia as both an energy source and an electron donor.

item.title: Mechanistic Classification of Multicatalysis
item.description: Multicatalysis combines two or more catalytic functions within a single reaction network and can unlock reactivity, selectivity, and synthetic efficiency that are difficult to achieve with an individual catalyst. Its mechanistic description, however, remains fragmented across partially overlapping terms such as tandem, relay, cooperative, synergistic, double-activation, and bifunctional catalysis, among others. Here, we propose a mechanism-first classification based on the relationship between catalytic functions and, specifically, on the catalytic ‘currency’ exchanged between them. When the currency is substrate-derived, the coupling is classified as tandem, cooperative, or double activation. When the exchanged currency controls catalyst state rather than contributing to the substrate framework (e.g. electrons, cofactors), the relationship is gated or regenerative, distinguished by whether activation is required only once or repeatedly during turnover. Importantly, the classification is additive, so complex reaction networks are represented as combinations of pairwise relationships. Representative reactions illustrate how this framework resolves mechanistic distinctions that are hidden by conventional labels. By linking nomenclature to the elementary connection between catalytic functions, the classification provides a compact language for comparing multicatalytic systems and a basis for more deliberate catalyst and reaction-network design.

item.title: Substituent Effects on Anion Bonding and Disassembly of Hypervalent Iodine Macrocycles
item.description: A series of phenylalanine-derived hypervalent iodine-based macrocycles (HIMs) bearing electron donating and withdrawing substituents were prepared. The HIM associations with the anion of tetrabutylammonium chloride (TBA-Cl) were systematically investigated using binding isotherms generated via NMR spectroscopy. The association constants of the resulting I-Cl bond were found to linearly correlate with the electronic substituents via Hammett analysis. Electron-withdrawing substituents strengthened the I–Cl bond and disassembled the macrocycle more readily. In addition, the shifting of HIM carbonyl frequencies obtained by Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy were found to correlate with the binding affinities and provide an alternative predictive methodology to determine HIM disassembly and anion binding affinities.

item.title: Conformational Heterogeneity and Local Electronic Structure in Wild-Type and Arctic Amyloid-Β42
item.description: Amyloid-𝛽 42 is a heterogeneous system, widely known as an intrinsically disordered protein, or IDP, sampling a variety of conformations. However, how ensemble redistribution affects the underlying local electronic structure remains less well understood. In this study, classical molecular dynamics simulations are combined with population-aware density functional theory and reduced active-space calculations to compare the LVFFA fragment of the wild-type and Arctic (E22G) variants. Common-space principal component analysis, clustering, and Ramachandran plot analysis depicted distinct trajectory distributions and greater conformational heterogeneity for the E22G trajectory. Population-ranked conformations representing 60.58% of WT and 54.98% of Arctic populations yielded conditional population-weighted B3LYP/def2-SVP HOMO-LUMO separations of 5.81 and 5.95 eV, respectively. The 0.14 eV Arctic–WT shift remained positive across moving-block bootstrap analyses. Fragment expansion altered frontier-orbital ordering, although the spatial character of LVFFA-associated states was preserved. CASCI tested active-space sensitivity, and matched UCCSD-VQE calculations reproduced CAS(4,4) CASCI reference energies for the reduced Hamiltonians. Together, these results demonstrate the importance of population-aware conformational sampling and model-definition sensitivity when relating heterogeneous biomolecular ensembles to quantum-chemical properties.

item.title: Assessing the Limits of He Isotope Separation Under
item.description: Separation of helium isotopes is of interest owing to the critical importance and limited supply of helium-3 (3He). Nanoporous materials offer a viable route for gas-phase isotope separation through either selective adsorption or quantum sieving. Here, to maximize the isotope selectivity of quantum sieving we propose coupling a strongly attracting open-metal site for He adsorption to a surrounding nanopore acting as a confining potential. We demonstrate that upon tightening the pore, the zero-point energy (ZPE) elevates up to a point where 3He detaches while 4He remains bound. Our model shows that 100% isotope-selective adsorption of 4He is achieved when pores of diameter 4.8-5.3 Å are coupled to metal sites with He binding energies of 2-20 kJ/mol. At 20 K, operating pressures between 0.3-30 bar are estimated, which increase to 2-6 kbar at 77 K. Even if the exact pore size for 100% isotope-selective adsorption cannot be realized, our results provide a rational design strategy for materials with unprecedentedly large He isotope separation factors at elevated temperatures.

item.title: Defining the Catalytic Boundaries of N-Nitrosourea-Forming StzF/SznF and Related Metalloenzymes through Genome Mining and Mechanistic Analysis
item.description: Enzymatic N–N bond formation is a rare and chemically challenging transformation in natural product biosynthesis. The non-heme iron metalloenzyme SznF catalyzes the formation of the N-nitrosourea pharmacophore of streptozotocin via the coordinated action of a diiron heme-oxygenase-like (HDO) domain and a mononuclear iron cupin domain. Although recent computational studies have advanced mechanistic models for this transformation, the determinants governing substrate specificity within this enzyme family remain poorly understood. Here, we employed a multi-pronged approach combining genome mining, substrate scope screening, protein engineering, structural analysis, and biochemical characterization to define the catalytic boundaries of SznF and related homologs. Genome mining identified a previously uncharacterized homolog displaying higher activity toward the native substrate Nω-methyl-L-arginine than SznF, expanding the known repertoire of N-nitrosourea-forming metalloenzymes. Comprehensive substrate screening further revealed the first non-native substrate accepted by this enzyme family, Nω-propyl-L-arginine, whereas all other modifications in carbon chain length, guanidino substitution, alkylation state, or stereochemistry did not result in detectable turnover. Structure-guided engineering that targeted the binding pocket surrounding the terminal alkyl substituent increased the activity of several variants toward Nω-propyl-L-arginine compared to wildtype SznF. Furthermore, cascade experiments, and nitric oxide supplementation further demonstrate that productive catalysis requires a precise combination of steric, electronic, and geometric features that cannot readily be compensated by alternative substrates. Together, these findings show that the substrate specificity of SznF and related homologs is governed by mechanistic constraints arising from the tightly coupled hydroxylation and rearrangement chemistry underlying N–N bond formation. More broadly, this work defines the catalytic boundaries of enzymatic N-nitrosourea formation while identifying new opportunities for the discovery and engineering of N–N bond-forming metalloenzymes for biocatalytic synthesis of structurally diverse N-nitrosourea derivatives.

item.title: A study of the valence shell photoionization dynamics following core level resonant excitation in imidazole
item.description: The photoionization and subsequent Auger decay dynamics of core-excited states in imidazole have been investigated at the carbon and nitrogen K-edges using linearly polarized synchrotron radiation. Ion yield measurements in the pre-edge regions were used to locate core-level transitions into either unoccupied valence or Rydberg states, and assignments were made through comparison with simulated spectra obtained using the RASPT2 method. Valence shell photoelectron spectra were recorded at photon energies coinciding with these core-level transitions, using two polarization orientations to allow the photoelectron angular distributions to be determined. The interpretation of these resonantly excited photoelectron spectra was guided by RASPT2 simulations that helped distinguish between participator and spectator contributions. Autoionization strongly affects the photoelectron intensity and angular distributions of the outer valence 1h states. Spectator contributions become evident at binding energies above 15 eV, and some of the intense 2h-1p states are well-described by the calculations, allowing assignments to be proposed. The non-resonantly excited C(KVV) and N(KVV) Auger spectra have been measured and some of the features at high kinetic energies have been assigned.

item.title: Density Functional Theory Bond Dissociation Energies of Model Compounds Relevant to LDL Oxidation: Bis-Allylic C–H, Phenolic O–H and Hydroperoxide O–H Bonds
item.description: Background: Oxidative modification of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) contributes to atherogenesis, with polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) as its main chemical target. Vitamin E is an effective chainbreaking antioxidant in vitro, yet large clinical trials showed no cardiovascular benefit. We calculated bond dissociation energies (BDEs) of model compounds to quantify the underlying thermodynamics. Methods: Density functional theory calculations (PySCF; B3LYP/6-311+G(d,p)//B3LYP/6-31G*, scaled zero-point energy, 0K) were performed for butane, 1,4-pentadiene, phenol, catechol and methyl hydroperoxide. Vitamin E was not calculated at the relaxed level; published values were used. A truncated tocopherol model (5,7,8-trimethylchroman-6-ol) was run at screening level only (B3LYP/6-31+G*, unrelaxed geometries, no zero-point correction), with phenol at the same level. Results: The bis-allylic C–H bond of 1,4-pentadiene (68.2 kcal/mol) was 28.3 below that of butane (96.5). Catechol O–H (73.4) was 8.4 below phenol (81.8). The hydroperoxide model (79.6) fell 2.2 below phenol, opposite to the approximate literature order; the cause was not investigated. In screening calculations the tocopherol model was 9.0 below phenol. Published values place α-tocopherol O–H at about 77 to 78 kcal/mol, about 10 below phenol, the same direction as our screening gap. Computed values were 1.7 to 8.6 kcal/mol below approximate literature values, so gaps and ordering, not absolute values, are interpreted. Conclusions: The calculations quantify the thermodynamic basis for PUFA vulnerability and for the stronger hydrogen donation of polyphenol-type O–H bonds. They do not by themselves show donation to peroxyl radicals. Bond energies cannot explain the clinical trial results; kinetics, LDL localization and tocopherol-mediated peroxidation must be considered. No clinical outcomes or biomarkers were computed.

item.title: Automated Extraction and FAIRification of Chemical Structures from Scientific Publications
item.description: Chemical structures are published predominantly as images, which makes them inaccessible for database indexing, structure-based search and computational reuse. While Optical Chemical Structure Recognition and PDF-extraction tools attempt post-publication recovery, they cannot restore the information lost during image rendering. To address this, we present BChemXtract, an open-source Java library that extracts chemical structures directly from the CDX and CDXML files that authors already submit with their manuscripts. BChemXtract parses the CDX object hierarchy to isolate chemical fragments from graphical annotations and expands abbreviations using a community-curated lookup table. The structures are then converted via the Chemistry Development Kit into standard machine-readable formats. BChemXtract is integrated into the production workflow of the Beilstein Journals, where extracted structures are manually validated before being embedded in article metadata as Schema.org JSON-LD, deposited in PubChem and offered for download. Applied to the 2993 ChemDraw figures and schemes of volume 20 of the Beilstein Journal of Organic Chemistry, it yielded 23,320 structures with InChIs in under two minutes. On a 225-file benchmark corpus, it generated valid InChIs for 98.2% of extracted unique substances, compared with 14.2% for Open Babel, at comparable per-file speed. BChemXtract makes published chemistry FAIR at the point of publication without altering author workflows. It is available under the MIT license together with a web application and the benchmark corpus.

item.title: Enhanced Sodium Metal Anode Cycling Stability via an Organometallic Electrolyte Additive
item.description: Despite the high theoretical capacity of sodium metal anodes, practical application is limited by the general instability of the solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) leading to dendritic growth and capacity fade. Here we report that the dimolybdenum paddlewheel complex, Mo2(mea)4 (1, mea = 2-(2-methoxyethoxy)acetate), functions as an effective electrolyte additive for Na metal anodes at millimolar loadings, enabled by self-assembly on the anode surface upon formation of aggregates involving 1 and Na+. In symmetric Na||Na cells, additive 1 was found to increase cycling stability and attenuate overpotential growth and impedance rise over 450 cycles compared to additive-free controls. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy revealed that 1 promotes early formation of an inorganic-rich SEI that also contains intact 1 and its downstream products. Scanning electron microscopy confirmed suppression of morphologies associated with dendrite growth. Full-cell Na||Na3V2(PO4)3 testing demonstrated improved Coulombic efficiency relative to an additive-free control and served to validate cathode compatibility of the additive. This work establishes organometallic complexes as an effective “third class” of Na metal battery additives, complementing purely organic or inorganic systems.

item.title: Detection and Characterization of the Cosmological Neutrino Background by EPR Spectroscopy on Molecular Hydrino with Implications for Telecommunications
item.description: A hydrino atom, H(1/p) solved using a Maxwellian electrodynamics and relativistic mechanics, is atomic hydrogen with state energy En = -13.598/n2 eV, in which n = 1/p, and p is limited by the energy in the electric field of the proton to 126 whereafter the proton and electron decay. Electron transitions to hydrino states involve an initial non-radiative energy transfer to a catalyst that serves as an energy hole or sink of a quantized amount of energy, 2mE1 (m is integer) to be transferred to a catalyst such as HOH, a free or nascent water molecule. Furthermore, hydrino atoms can react to form the corresponding diatomic molecule referred to as molecular hydrino H2(1/p). In contrast to molecular hydrogen (H2), the molecular hydrino (H2(1/p)) is paramagnetic with S = ½ comprising a paired and unpaired electron in the same MO wherein the lower energy state central field is provided by photons akin to gluons in nucleons in addition to the field of the protons. Due to its unique structure, H2(1/p)) interacts with the neutrinos in the energy range of the cosmological neutrino background (𝐶𝜈𝐵) as confirmed by the neutrino mediated observations of predicted fine structure, predicted high magnetic field Paschen Beck effect, large downfield shifts, temporal changes of EPR spectra due to accumulated changes in fine structure state populations, extraordinary broadened signals, zero order absorption occurring in the perpendicular and parallel modes, and the observation of magnetic dipole-dipole interactions of H2(1/4)-H2 dimer requiring intramolecular angular momentum transfer from a neutrino excited fine structure state in H2(1/4) as well as unique temperature and matrix dependences of the EPR signals. EPR was used to detect and characterize the 𝐶𝜈𝐵 for the first time. The isotropic and parallel propagation nature of 𝐶𝜈𝐵 can be exploited for line of site telecommunications requiring no transmission power to transmit signals in any direction unattenuated and undispersed through any physical barrier, including the Earth.

item.title: Tuning the Anchoring and ORR Activity of Sub-Nano Pt Clusters on HOPG via Ion Implantation and Oxygen Functionalization
item.description: Sub-nanometer supported clusters are of interest in catalysis due to nearly complete precious metal atom utilization, generally high catalytic activity, and attractive tunability via size and clustersupport interactions. The stability of such clusters remains a challenge, however. We demonstrate anchoring and stabilization of size-selected Ptn, n = 2 - 10 clusters soft-landed on HOPG, achieved 2 by modifying the HOPG with 100 eV kinetic energy N(𝑛 1, 2) and Ar+ ions, with and without O2 oxidation of the ion-modified surfaces, prior to Ptn soft-landing. Ion modification is found to significantly improve the sticking probability for soft-landed Ptn, implying increased adsorption energies, and O2 exposure prior to cluster deposition increases the sticking probability to ~unity. DFT finds that Ptn bind preferentially to under-coordinated carbon sites created by the ion impacts, rather than to implanted N atoms, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and scanning tunneling microscopy both show that the defect-anchored clusters are stable against sintering. There is net electron transfer from the defect-bound clusters to the support, and the local defect structure may undergo significant restructuring due to Pt-C bond formation. To probe the effects of ion-modified HOPG on the chemical properties of the adsorbed Ptn clusters, we tested electrodes prepared by Ptn deposition on ion-modified HOPG for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR). The ion-modified electrodes showed ORR activity consistent with cluster size being maintained, and O2 modification enhanced both cluster anchoring and ORR activity. Thus, ion modification provides means to stabilize sub-nano cluster electrodes, while oxygen functionalization of the anchoring sites tunes the electrocatalytic activity.

item.title: Size-Controlled HgTe Nanocrystals Achieve Near-Unity Shortwave Infrared Emission
item.description: The near-infrared (NIR, 700-1000 nm) and short-wave infrared (SWIR, 1000-2000 nm) regions of light are privileged for optoelectronic applications due to the decreased scattering and diminished autofluorescence arising from the few natural chromophores which absorb or emit in these windows. We demonstrate a two-stage, size-resolved synthesis of spherical HgTe quantum dots (QDs) with narrowband photoluminescence tunable across the NIR and SWIR which combine exceptionally high photoluminescence quantum yields (QY > 80%), low polydispersity (<10%), and stability in air. Using this synthetic control, we determine the size-dependent bandgap and molar extinction coefficients of HgTe under extreme confinement, and show conclusively that separating nucleation from growth — via a fast injection followed by a slow one — suppresses Ostwald ripening. Post-synthetic incubation with zinc salts further improves optical stability, pushing QY to near unity across the SWIR, including at telecom-relevant wavelengths. We then formulate water-soluble HgTe QD micelles as contrast agents for in vivo mouse imaging in the SWIR, achieving 100 frame/s video-rate imaging above 1400 nm with contrast and temporal resolution that substantially exceed those of indocyanine green. Together, these results establish that even without a protective shell, HgTe QDs offer a near-optimal, air-stable platform for optoelectronic applications at telecom-relevant wavelengths.

item.title: Density Functional Theory of Dion-Jacobson Double Perovskite Halides
item.description: First-principles density functional theory was used to study six (four unreported) hybrid layered double perovskites of the Dion-Jacobson A2MM ′′′ X8 family. All 6 compounds consist of organic diamines that bridge rock-saltordered inorganic octahedra, with Ag+ as the M ′ site and Bi+3/Sb+3 as the M′′′ site. Both aliphatic (1,3-diaminopropane [PDA], 1,4-diaminobutane [BDA], 1,8-diaminooctane [ODA]) and aromatic (para-phenylenediamine [PPDA]) spac-ers are investigated, revealing how composition affects the band gap character and magnitude. Formation energy analysis using the DFT-D3 method reveals negative formation energies with respect to relevant precursors. Furthermore, calculations using the complex dielectric function reveal key optical properties, including absorption coefficients, refractive indices, and complex permittivity.

item.title: Phosphorus(V) Umpolung Converts Electrophilic Phosphates into Nucleophilic H-Phosphonates
item.description: Ubiquitous in chemistry, biology and medicine, phosphate groups form the backbone of DNA and RNA, and their analogues like phosphorothioate antisense oligonucleotides provide frontier therapies for challenging genetic disorders. However, the inherent electrophilicity of phosphorus(V) and thermodynamic stability of native P–OH bonds preclude their direct, latestage conversion into phosphate analogues. Here, we introduce a polarity-reversal (umpolung) strategy for converting electrophilic phosphates into nucleophilic H-phosphonates. This approach proceeds through two stages: P–OH thiolation into a thiophosphate followed by radical P–S cleavage, which generates the P–H bond. This sequence converts diverse phosphate substrates, such as complex drug scaffolds and nucleotides, into H-phosphonates that can undergo further phosphorus functionalization. The thiolation step also enables direct, one-pot conversion of P–OH into P–SH in nucleotides, providing a chemical route to the phosphorothioation of native phosphate backbones associated with bacterial and archaeal DNA defense. Therefore, phosphorus(V) umpolung reverses the polarity of phosphate chemistry, transforming otherwise stable P–OH bonds into synthetically versatile phosphorus functionalities.

item.title: Complementary Roles of Iodide-Mediated Pathways and Anion Dynamics in Lithium-Ion Transport in Li3PS4-LiI Glasses
item.description: LiI addition enhances lithium-ion transport in sulfide glasses, yet the microscopic mechanisms linking halide incorporation to faster conduction remain unclear. Here, we investigate how LiI promotes Li+ migration in (100−x)Li3PS4–xLiI glasses by resolving changes in local structure, migration energetics, and anion dynamics. A machinelearning potential trained on newly generated ab initio molecular dynamics data and an existing sulfide-electrolyte dataset enables 10 ns simulations of approximately 5000atom glass models at 300 K over a LiI content range of 0–50 mol%. The potential is validated against density functional theory calculations, experimental densities, and X-ray total scattering profiles. Although the PS4 3–units remain intact and their time-averaged inter-unit correlations change little, Li+ diffusivity more than doubles across this composition range, accompanied by increased migration beyond local cage-like regions. To characterize the energetics of these pathways in a disordered environment, we introduce an analysis that combines Voronoi partitioning into P-and I–-centered domains with atomic potentialenergy fluctuations along Li+ trajectories. The resulting statistical local energy-barrier indicators allow comparisons between domain transitions without assigning absolute activation energies. This analysis reveals two complementary effects of LiI addition. Transitions involving I–-centered domains exhibit lower barrier indicators than direct transitions between P-centered domains, identifying favorable I–-mediated migration pathways. LiI addition also lowers the barrier indicators for direct P-to-P transitions, extending its influence beyond pathways that pass through I–-centered domains. Enhanced local translational and rotational dynamics of PS4 3–units accompany this broader reduction, suggesting that anion motion helps facilitate Li+ migration. These findings explain how LiI can enhance transport while largely preserving the average glass structure and highlight the combined roles of local migration pathways and anion dynamics in designing sulfide glass electrolytes.

item.title: Customizable Approach to Conformer Space Discretization using Torsion Angular Bin Strings (customTABS)
item.description: Conformational ensembles of small organic molecules are primarily determined by the rotameric states of their torsional or dihedral angles. The previously introduced concept of torsion angular bin strings (TABS) is a discrete vector representation of a molecule’s dihedral states, which therefore offer a quantitative description of such ensembles. Discretization of the torsional-angle space allows us to count distinct conformational states, giving an estimate of the upper limit of the expected conformational ensemble size (nTABS). In addition to nTABS being used as a qualitative measure of molecular flexibility, TABS itself is a way of grouping conformers of a molecule without picking thresholds. In the initial version of the TABS application, the discretization was based on crystal-structure derived torsion preferences, which may not be fully transferable to the conformational preferences in other environments. Here, we present the extension of the TABS framework to consider observed, system-specific distributions for the discretization of the conformational space. CustomTABS can be used to decompose the given conformational ensemble into the torsional states, which can be useful for clustering, importance ranking of dihedrals, or convergence analysis. We present the algorithmic solutions developed for the customTABS extension and demonstrate their application in clustering molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories and monitoring the convergence of the observed torsional space.

item.title: Solvent Dynamics and Multiconfigurational Treatment Drive the Anomalous Stokes Shift of HINA
item.description: The 3-hydroxyisonicotinaldehyde (HINA) anion is one of the smallest known green-emissive fluorophores, yet the origin of its anomalously large Stokes shift (0.87 eV) remains unexplained. Given the well-established influence of the surrounding environment on the photophysical properties of fluorescent dyes, we examine its role in this shift by simulating the anion's absorption and emission spectra with four computational protocols that differ in configurational sampling, solvent treatment, and electronic-structure method. Wigner sampling protocols capture less than half of the experimental Stokes shift, whether the solvent is treated implicitly or explicitly, whereas QM/MM molecular dynamics sampling improves it significantly. Structural analysis associates this improvement with coupling between the first solvation shell and the intramolecular interaction between the aldehyde hydrogen and the hydroxyl oxygen, which is captured by molecular-dynamics sampling but not by the corresponding frozen-solute Wigner-sampling protocol. When combined with RMS-CASPT2, this sampling quantitatively reproduces the experimental spectra and Stokes shift (0.85 versus 0.87 eV), showing that quantitative description of the Stokes shift of HINA requires both solvent-induced conformational dynamics and a multiconfigurational electronic-structure treatment.

item.title: Chromoselective Control for Aminoalkylation of CF3‑Alkenes through Low-Energy Photoredox Catalysis
item.description: Recent advances in chromoselective photoredox catalysis have demonstrated that light wavelength can serve as a powerful and orthogonal reaction parameter, enabling divergent reactivity from a single catalytic system. Building on recent advances in the sequential decarboxylative/defluorinative aminoalkylation of trifluoromethyl-substituted alkenes, we report a divergent, wavelength-dependent strategy for the site-selective functionalization of N-arylglycines. High-throughput experimentation (HTE) was used to systematically screen photocatalysts and irradiation wavelengths to identify the most suitable divergent conditions. Interestingly, using [Ru(bpy)3]2+ as photocatalyst, irradiation with blue light promotes efficient difunctionalization of CF3-alkenes with N-arylglycines, affording monofluoroalkenyl-1,5-diamines, while switching the irradiation to red light enables selective monofunctionalization, delivering the corresponding gem-difluoroalkenyl amine intermediates exclusively under otherwise identical conditions, via a spin-forbidden transition pathway. This wavelength-governed switchable reactivity provides a powerful and tunable platform for the controlled radical modification of amino acids, expanding the synthetic utility of visible-light photoredox catalysis in divergent amine synthesis. Mechanistic investigations using photoelectrochemistry and TD-DFT have revealed notably a photo-excitation of intermediates, allowing for the second functionalization to whether happens or not, based on the irradiation wavelength used.

item.title: Free induction decay-detected high-field electron spin resonance for accurate monitoring highly polarized spin dynamics
Utilization of heuristic approaches and molecular modelling to visualise chemical reactivity in small student groups
item.description: According to current psychometric analyses, a vast majority of novices in universities mostly utilize algorithmic mental processes to solve given tasks and tests. Although algorithmic thinking is an essential part of brain functions, experts on didactics call for methods which also develop conceptual thinking in beginners. In this sense, heuristic molecular modelling plays an important role in chemistry education since it inherently employs several conceptual thinking principles. Herein, we present eight different molecular modelling tasks of Diels-Alder reactions to develop understanding of the concept of chemical reactivity in undergraduate students of chemistry. The aim of this study is to provide teachers of chemistry with an example lesson utilizing heuristic education techniques and molecular modelling. The present study was evaluated in a university course on advanced organic chemistry for students in the third year of a chemistry master program. Interviews with the involved students and analyses of the applied pre/post didactical tests show that the proposed lesson has a positive impact on the understanding of basic chemical concepts related with chemical reactivity and Diels-Alder reaction.

item.title: Solid-phase synthesis and structure-degradation relationships of VHL-recruiting PROTACs for preferential histone deacetylase 6 degradation
item.description: This work reports on a series of von Hippel-Lindau (VHL)-recruiting histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6) PROTACs based on a vorinostat-inspired HDAC inhibitor. Systematic variations of the VHL ligand, the exit vector, and the linker architecture revealed that longer, semi-rigid linkers promoted efficient HDAC6 degradation. Compounds 12-15 emerged as potent HDAC6 degraders, with 15 exhibiting a half-maximal degradation value of 26 nM with 12 showing particularly rapid degradation kinetics. The lead compounds induced pronounced and preferential HDAC6 degradation in MM.1S and FLT3-ITD-positive MV4-11 cells. Notably, 13-15 displayed submicromolar antiproliferative activity in MV4-11 cells and significantly induced apoptosis. Compound 13 was markedly more active than its non-degrading control nc-13, despite nearly identical HDAC1 and HDAC6 inhibitory activities, which underscores the important contribution of targeted HDAC degradation to the antiproliferative activity. Overall, this study supports VHL-mediated targeted degradation as a promising strategy to translate HDAC6 targeting into pronounced antileukemic activity.

item.title: Pathway Reweighting in DNA Reaction Networks Enables Adaptation to Environmental Pressures
item.description: Adaptive biochemical reaction networks must respond to environmental changes while maintaining function, yet synthetic networks typically rely on predefined pathways and stimulus–response relationships. Here, we introduce pathway reweighting as a strategy for adaptivity in DNA strand-displacement reaction networks. We design a splitting network in which two competing pathways connect a shared initial state to a common output. This allows environmental perturbations to redistribute reaction flux between the pathways while preserving overall network function. We showcase environmental sensitivity by integrating pHresponsive i-motif and ATP-binding aptamer motifs that enable selective and proportional adaptation. Combining these pressures demonstrates pathway reweighting under more complex, biologically relevant environmental conditions. Beyond proportional adaptation, we introduce a distinct, history-dependent mechanism based on an enzymatic feed-forward loop. The loop progressively modifies the Input strand, creating delayed pathway reweighting and encoding a memory of prior environmental exposure. A deep-learning reaction-network framework resolves the resulting interconnected dynamics and identifies changes in pathway utilization without requiring complete mechanistic parameterization. Our experimentalnumerical framework enables the rational design of synthetic CRNs whose adaptive behavior emerges from network organization rather than explicit reaction-by-reaction programming.

item.title: Drug Molecular and Route Similarity-Aware Retrieval-Augmented LLM Generation with Knowledge Graph for Semantic Reasoning
item.description: To address the inherent limitations of large language models (LLMs) in chemical synthesis—hallucinations, and low knowledge dense—this study presents a Knowledge Graph–enhanced Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework (KG-RAG-LLM) with a multi-scale calculation of molecular and route similarity. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that KG-RAG-LLM significantly mitigates hallucinations, increasing the proportion of concrete chemical information in generated responses to 39.52%–40.87%, drastically outperforming baseline LLMs and standard literature-based RAG pipelines in response completeness and accuracy. To overcome the inability of traditional 2D linear fingerprints to capture 3D spatial properties and reaction path variations, we further developed a multidimensional molecular and route similarity calculation combining SimHash, core similarity, and FCFP, as an alternative to Route CGR representations coupled with UMAP dimensionality reduction. This formulation accurately distinguishes between subtle and distinct synthetic strategies, demonstrating superior precision over traditional clustering methods for fuzzy retrieval of synthetic routes. Overall, this work provides a reliable, knowledge-dense solution for intelligent retrosynthetic Semantic Reasoning.

item.title: Commit: Automated Scale-Up Crystallisation DataFactory for model-based pharmaceutical process development: a data-driven, mechanistic and hybrid model case study
item.description: In 2025, we introduced the Scale-Up Crystallisation DataFactory, an automated platform for crystallisation experimentation and Bayesian optimisation. However, the initial case study used a relatively simple three-parameter, single-objective optimisation problem. In this Commit paper, we extend the platform to a five-dimensional, multi-objective cooling-antisolvent crystallisation of lovastatin and benchmark data-driven, mechanistic and hybrid optimisation approaches. Sixteen screening experiments were followed by model-guided experiments targeting yield and particle size (D90). Bayesian optimisation produced continued improvements in hypervolume, while mechanistic and hybrid approaches did not improve experimental performance beyond screening. The results demonstrate the value of experimentally benchmarking optimisation strategies for autonomous process development.

item.title: Removal of Cu(II) and a PET Glitter Microplastic Surrogate by Alginate, Alginate–Opuntia, and Chitosan-Treated Alginate–Opuntia Beads
item.description: The use of alginate-only beads, alginate–Opuntia (AO) beads, and chitosan-treated AO beads for the removal of Cu(II) and a PET glitter (a microplastic surrogate) from water has been investigated. Each bead type was made from the previous one by the addition of one component. Batch experiments were carried out in water containing glitter, Cu(II), or both, and AO beads soaked in dilute acetic acid without chitosan served as a control for the acid. The removal of Cu(II) in copper-only water was 45.71 ± 1.97%, 59.44 ± 2.28%, and 84.19 ± 2.65% for the alginate-only, AO, and chitosan-treated beads, respectively (mean ± SD, n = 12, 6 h, 140 rpm). Opuntia increased the Cu(II) removal by 13.72 percentage points and chitosan by a further 24.75 points (paired t-test, p < 0.001 for both, and p ≤ 0.0013 for the batch means). In the presence of 2.00 g of glitter, the chitosan-treated beads still removed about 84% of the Cu(II). Meanwhile, the glitter removal increased by about 7 points with Opuntia but changed by less than 0.25 points with chitosan (p = 0.648 and 0.231). No significant difference was found between the acid-soaked and the untreated AO beads. It can be concluded that Opuntia was responsible for the increase in glitter capture and chitosan for most of the increase in Cu(II) removal.

item.title: Toward bio-circular, fully organic batteries from non-toxic and bio-derived materials
item.description: The development of biodegradable energy storage systems is essential for enabling environmental monitoring devices that can degrade after stable operation. In this work, we present a fully organic, bio-circular battery that uses materials selected using a framework based on their natural occurrence and hazard classification according to the Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals (GHS). We use redox-active organic molecules, aloe-emodin and luteolin, immobilized on activated coconut charcoal, together with an agarose/carboxymethyl cellulose gel polymer electrolyte and current collectors based on graphite flakes, carbon black, and agarose. The resulting battery delivers 0.7 V and stable electrochemical performance, supplying 8.8 mAh/g after 200 cycles, with 73.6% capacity retention and 98% coulombic efficiency. All components are further integrated into a pouch cell with an agarose packaging and beeswax coating. This prototype exhibits a discharge capacity of 7.1 μAh and 77.9% capacity retention over 20 cycles. Under simulated aerobic composting conditions, the pouch cell shows rapid and substantial disintegration, highlighting its potential for environmentally benign end-of-life scenarios. This work establishes a comprehensive design strategy for bio-circular batteries and demonstrates the applicability of bio-derived, GHS-non-toxic, fully organic materials for sustainable energy storage solutions.

item.title: Process and Systems Modeling of Hydrothermal Liquefaction for Fuels and Bioproducts from Wet Organic Wastes
item.description: Hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) can convert wet organic waste into fuels and bioproducts, but variation in feedstocks and operating conditions can propagate from product yields to system performance and deployment. This study linked machine learning based HTL yield prediction with process simulation, techno-economic analysis (TEA), life cycle assessment (LCA), uncertainty analysis, and surrogate modeling. A literature data set of 402 experiments was used to predict biocrude, aqueous, gas, and solids yields, with 71.8% of predictions within ±5 wt% of experimental values. The predicted yields reproduced 77.1% of internal rate of return (IRR) and 83.2% of GWP100 estimates within ±5% and ±10 kg CO2e/kg, respectively, and were integrated into two deployment configurations (centralized and decentralized HTL) and two product pathways (biobinder/biofuel and sustainable aviation fuel [SAF]). Process and system scale analyses showed that operating conditions strongly affecting HTL performance could have weaker or competing economic effects due to tradeoffs among product yields, water handling, energy requirements, and capital costs. Across representative feedstocks, decentralized biobinder systems achieved median IRRs up to 35.8%, compared with up to 8.0% for decentralized SAF systems. Feedstock price, followed by biocrude quality, and biocrude yield emerged as the leading economic drivers. Monte Carlo filtering identified waste tipping fee thresholds $25.1–196.7 per wet metric tonne for achieving the 10% IRR target. These results show that existing tipping fee structure can support HTL deployment in some cases, while higher tipping fees or additional financial incentives can expand viability and enable higher investment returns.

item.title: The role of membrane properties and environmental footprint in shaping the cost-climate optimal carbon capture processes
item.description: Membrane development for carbon capture is typically guided by CO2 permeability and CO2/N2 selectivity, although these properties alone cannot determine whether a material will deliver economically and environmentally favourable performance at scale. Herein, we develop a multi-criteria optimization framework that integrates a machine-learning surrogate model of a multi-stage membrane process with techno-economic analysis and life cycle assessment. By applying this framework to mixed matrix membranes, we investigate the interplay of membrane properties and membrane-specific inventories in defining process-level costs and environmental indicators. For the capture from flue gases produced by a waste incinerator plant and a cement plant, electricity is mostly driven by CO2/O2 selectivity within the investigated range and is the dominant contributor to process costs and climate change impacts. This makes the climate benefits of membrane-based capture strongly dependent on the electricity supply: high-performance membranes supplied with carbon-intensive electricity can have climate change impacts comparable to or even higher than those of low-performing membranes supplied with low-carbon electricity. Therefore, we show for the first time how the system-level context shapes the properties that must be prioritized and their target values to unlock economic and environmental benefits: membrane synthesis and lifetime have a substantial impact in the presence of clean electricity, whereas increasingly high CO2/O2 and CO2/N2 selectivity are needed in the presence of moderate to high carbon intensity. Overall, with this work, we identify priorities for improvement in membrane production and performance that could only be revealed by jointly considering process-level costs and environmental impacts.

item.title: Building the Data Foundations for the Design and Discovery of Transition Metal Complexes
item.description: The unique chemistry of transition metal complexes (TMCs) enables several advanced technologies in diverse fields including renewable energies, medicine, and catalysis. Machine learning methods can accelerate their rational design but are bounded by limited dataset sizes, restricted chemical scopes, and insufficient quality. This Perspective surveys the current landscape of TMC datasets and investigates how they seek to address these challenges. The analysis focuses on the data curation processes as well as the scope of the properties provided, and their level of theory. Furthermore, the applications and methodological advancements enabled by TMC datasets are reviewed, including the generative design of metal ligands and the evolutionary optimization of TMCs. The Perspective concludes by outlining future directions, with particular emphasis on extending data to broader chemical scopes including non-equilibrium geometries, establishing community-wide data formats and benchmarks, and developing strategies to effectively integrate heterogeneous data sources.

item.title: Cholesteric Liquid Crystals for Ultratrace PFAS Detection
item.description: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent, mobile water contaminants associated with adverse effects on human health and ecosystems. Current analytical methods require specialized instrumentation, complicating their on-site detection at ultratrace concentrations across distributed water infrastructures. Here we integrate fluorophilic partitioning and proton-responsive recognition within a cholesteric liquid crystal (CLC). The fluorinated component promotes selectivity over non-fluorinated structural analogues, whereas the pyridine receptor transduces protonation into changes in helical organization and reflected color. The formulation was confined within monodisperse spherical droplets and processed as a photocurable photonic ink to produce sensing strips with a strong reflection signal readable by portable fiber-optic spectroscopy. The platform detected five PFAS through concentration-dependent blue-shifts, reaching detection limits of 5.9 parts per trillion (ppt) without sample preconcentration and maintaining comparable performance across three water matrices. Coupling molecular recognition to collective supramolecular reorganization establishes CLCs as promising sensing materials for on-site ultratrace PFAS detection.

item.title: Electrochemical Capture of Microplastics via Reversible Metal Deposition in Aqueous Solutions
item.description: Microplastics are persistent aqueous contaminants for which effective removal strategies remain needed. Here, we investigate electrochemical deposition as a means of capturing suspended polystyrene (PS) particles. The purpose of this study is to understand the plausibility of electrochemical deposition as a means for removing microplastics from aqueous systems. The central hypothesis guiding this work is that ramified solid metallic deposits created during electrodeposition can mechanically capture plastic particles suspended in the liquid phase. PS particles of 200 nm and 250 μm were evaluated in ZnSO4 electrolyte under applied potentials from 0 to −4 V, with surfactant conditions also examined. Electrochemical treatment resulted in visibly reduced turbidity, suggesting a decrease in suspended particle concentration. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) showed particles attached to or incorporated within deposited zinc. Particle capture was not observed at 0 V but was evident under active zinc deposition at −2 V, supporting the role of electrodeposited zinc in particle capture. The observed particle–electrode interactions differed with particle size: larger particles were partially embedded within rough, dendritic zinc deposits, whereas nanoscale particles were densely distributed across the deposited structure. These observations demonstrate the ability of electrodeposition to facilitate particle capture through distinct particle–deposit interactions and support its potential as a tunable approach for investigating microplastic capture in aqueous systems.

item.title: COSMO-RS-Based Theoretical Investigation of Equilibria in Protic Ionic Liquids
item.description: Ionic liquids have become an increasingly important field of research. A subgroup, protic ionic liquids, have been shown to be excellent solvents even for poorly soluble materials such as cellulose or polyamides. Still, the composition of such liquids, e.g., their ionicity and the nature of formed aggregates, is mostly unknown and experimental attempts to shed light on this have been mostly unsuccessful. Herein, we report the development of the Python-based COSMOPIL program (COnductor-like Screening MOdel for Protic Ionic Liquids) to analyze the composition of protic ionic liquids via theoretical methods based on density functional theory (DFT) and the COSMO-RS (COnductor-like Screening MOdel for Real Solvents) implicit solvation model. The inputs of experimental data such as dielectric constants is not necessary. The COSMO-PIL program demonstrates the influence of acid/base ratios and residual water on the ionic liquid composition and allows the understanding of the reported poor ionicity of those liquids. Most notably, we explain this “ionicity gap” in protic ionic liquids, as even superbases fail to achieve full acid deprotonation, with a polarity mismatch between anion and cation, requiring residual acid as mediator.

item.title: A hydrochromic porous aromatic framework for self-reporting, high-capacity atmospheric water harvesting
item.description: Atmospheric water harvesting materials are typically optimised for sorption performance alone, despite the practical importance of monitoring sorbent loading. Here, we report a hydrochromic porous aromatic framework that integrates water capture and self-reporting within a single adaptive material. Sulfonation of PAF-1 affords the hydrophilic framework PAF-1-S that adsorbs 0.18 g·g-1 of water at only 10% RH and reaches 1.87 g·g-1 at 90% RH, combining exceptional low-humidity capture with the highest total capacity among the porous sorbents surveyed here. Water adsorption simultaneously induces a reversible, graded colour change, enabling direct visualisation of sorbent loading without external sensing hardware. Spectroscopic analysis indicates that this response arises from hydration-driven acid–base equilibria within the modified framework. Combined with rapid sorption kinetics, low-temperature regeneration and robust cycling stability, these findings establish responsive porous adsorbents as a strategy for intelligent sorption materials.

item.title: Late-Stage Ligand Prioritization by Combining Rapid-Dissociation Filtering with MM/GBSA
item.description: Accurate and efficient prediction of binding free energies remains a central challenge in computational chemistry, largely due to the complexity of solvent effects and the trade-off between accuracy and computational cost. Explicit solvent molecular dynamics (MD) simulations provide detailed thermodynamic and kinetic insight, now routinely reaching microsecond timescales, while end-point methods such as MM/GBSA offer high efficiency but are sensitive to model parameters. In particular, the accuracy of MM/GBSA strongly depends on the atomic radii used to define the dielectric boundary within the implicit solvent framework. Here, we introduce an explicit–implicit hybrid workflow for late-stage ligand prioritization that integrates the strengths of both approaches. In this framework, microsecond-scale explicit solvent MD simulations act as a rapid-dissociation filter, flagging weak or unstable binders through spontaneous dissociation within the simulation window. MM/GBSA is then used to rank the remaining candidates. To improve the accuracy of the implicit solvent stage, we employ optimized atomic radii sets (OPTBIND), specifically designed for binding free-energy calculations. On the protein–ligand complexes of Curated32-4 set , a new curated benchmark of 32 complexes including 4 congeneric series, the entropy-free MM/GBSA stage with OPT- BIND 6D achieved Pearson r = 0.82 and Spearman ρ = 0.84, with 100% recovery of the experimental rank ordering across all four congeneric series, while a single-replica consistency test of the rapid-dissociation filter yielded an AUC of 0.88 and retained all 15 sub-micromolar binders. Finally, as a real-world drug design application, we apply the workflow to halogen substitutions in SARS-CoV-2 main protease inhibitors, demonstrating its ability to identify favorable chemical modifications. Notably, the approach prospectively identifies F→Cl and F→I as affinity-enhancing substitutions; the predicted enhancement for the chlorine analog is subsequently confirmed experimentally, while the iodine analog remains a testable prediction, highlighting its predictive power in guiding chemical optimization. Together, these results establish a practical framework for detailed studies of receptor–ligand binding and for late-stage ligand prioritization in drug discovery.

item.title: Characterisation of thermostable CYP116B reductase domains as modular electron transfer units for redox biocatalysis
item.description: Electron transfer is a common bottleneck in redox biocatalysis. Here, we report the isolation of five cytochrome P450 reductase (CPR) domains from the thermophilic, self-sufficient CYP116B family. These enzymes have considerable industrial potential because their CPR and haem domains are naturally fused, yet the catalytic properties of the individual components remain poorly understood. EPR and UV–Vis spectroscopy confirmed the canonical FMN and [2Fe–2S] cofactors were present, although occupancy varied (FMN, 30–62%; [2Fe–2S], 10–33%). The isolated CPRs were generally stable, robust and electron-transfer competent, supporting electrochemical NADPH/NADP+ oxidation/reduction and NADPH-driven reduction of ferric cytochrome c. All homologues were more thermostable than the CPR from non-thermophilic CYP116B2, with stability showing an apparent correlation with [2Fe-2S] occupancy. Separating the CPR and haem domains generally reduced the ability to perform hydroxylation on a model substrate (diclofenac). However, isolated AxCPR and AxHAEM formed a productive non-covalent combination with activity comparable to the full-length enzyme (TON 439.38 ± 5.19 versus 416.43 ± 12.11). Given the widespread use of CYP116B CPR domains as surrogate redox partners in P450 catalysis, these findings provide valuable insight into their catalytic performance. Furthermore, the results demonstrate the potential of the isolated CYP116B CPRs as modular electron-transfer units for redox biocatalysis more widely.

item.title: UpKast: Method, Model, and Database for Large-Scale Cross-Solvent Determination of pKa Values
item.description: The acid dissociation constant, commonly written as pKa, plays a key role in chemistry. However, most pKa measurements have been conducted in only a handful of solvents, resulting in data scarcity for many relevant solvent systems. Herein, we introduce the UpKast-DB, which comprises of pKa estimates for around 3,000 acids and bases in 29 solvents. We constructed UpKast-DB using a quantum-chemical method that integrates solvation free energy calculations with experimental data. Furthermore, we trained a surrogate machine learning model UpKast-ML on the computed values, allowing for rapid and accurate prediction of pKa values beyond the acids and bases presented in UpKast-DB. The quantum-chemical and machine learning methods result in RMSEs of approximately 1 pKa unit relative to experimental values, slightly higher than the typical aleatoric uncertainty of underlying experimental data, but more accurate than many existing experimental measurements (which can have uncertainties up to, and sometimes beyond, 3 pKa units). The data and modeling approaches provide a means of productively augmenting existing pKa data sources, and represent a significant step toward general determination of pKa in any solvent. The dataset and models can be found on Zenodo: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23239570

item.title: CP-GFM-SGX: Topology-Aware Cyclic Peptide Generation and Design with Receptor-Conditioned Structural Evaluation and Experimental KRAS Affinity Optimization
item.description: Cyclic-peptide discovery requires molecular topology, atomic structure, receptor-associated evidence and computational decisions to remain consistent across a multistage workflow. We present CP-GFM-SGX, an all-atom generative AI model for cyclic-peptide design that integrates a topology-aware generative core with a Unified Evidence State Machine (UESM) to track candidate identity, chemical validity, provenance, typed failures and bounded computation. We evaluated three distinct aspects of the system. In Track A, a frozen five-complex known-ligand benchmark with 100 scheduled poses per complex, the native-free FULL route selected a ligand-backbone pose with root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) below 2 Å in four of five systems; retrospective best-of-100 evaluation found a sub-2-Å pose in all five (median selected RMSD, 1.72 Å). In Track B, matched true-pocket versus shuffled-pocket comparisons favored the specified pocket in all seven main targets (median of target medians, +172.6 Rosetta energy units; weakest margin, +3.9 for MCL-1–9CDT). An exploratory post-protocol assessor admitted 42/42, 42/42 and 40/42 selected top-K slots in the full, condition-masked and post hoc head-to-tail arms, respectively. In Track C, FULL UESM produced the specified protective outcomes for six deterministic synthetic fault fixtures and one additional missing-evidence case; targeted ablations isolated the roles of provenance and failure propagation. In a separate KRAS G12D–GDP experimental-feedback series, synthesis and SPR/BLI testing of cyclic-peptide analogues guided position-2 basic-side-chain selection and dual-basic-group placement, advancing the reported SPR affinity from approximately 60 µM for CRO-748 to approximately 6 µM for 748-R1 and approximately 1 µM for 748-RK. Comparisons using the 31-dimension Structured Capability and Evidence Grid (SCEG-31D) demonstrate that CP-GFM-SGX exhibits certain superiority over other design platforms in multiple aspects. Together, we evaluate a topology-aware generative artificial intelligence workflow for receptor-focused cyclic-peptide design and show, in a KRAS feedback series, how binding measurements guide iterative chemical optimization.

item.title: Directional Prediction Errors Reveal Systematic Underprediction of Low-Pressure Carbon Dioxide Adsorption in Compact Metal–Organic Frameworks
item.description: A prediction residual has both magnitude and sign, yet materials-screening studies usually treat only its magnitude as informative. Here we show that residual sign localizes systematic underprediction of low-pressure carbon dioxide (CO2) adsorption to a compact, low-accessibility region of metalorganic-framework (MOF) descriptor space. We analyze 7,306 MOFs in a topology-held-out test set, keeping related framework topologies out of training. A one-sided 90% calibration defines the expected underprediction tail; critically, that tail is not distributed uniformly across materials space. Strong-underprediction incidence falls from 27.6% to 4.0% across accessible-volume-fraction quintiles and from 26.5% to 2.7% across accessible-surface-area quintiles, while rising from 4.2% to 24.7% with density. Individual discrepancies reach 6.35 mmol g−1. Literature-derived structural annotations of leading Mg-and Ca-containing cases motivate the testable hypothesis that global geometric descriptors can miss favorable first adsorption environments in compact frameworks; they do not establish a distinct microscopic adsorption mechanism. A calibrated lower-bound screen provides a separate practical corollary for conservative candidate prioritization. The central result is not the expected size of a positive-error tail, but its structured location in descriptor space. Retaining residual direction therefore provides a chemically interpretable diagnostic of model failure and identifies the next discriminating calculation or experiment.

item.title: Zr-MOF/Quinone Multicatalysis Enables Programmable Aerobic Synthesis of Benzimidazoles
item.description: Selectivity control in aerobic oxidation reactions containing several oxidizable functional groups remains challenging. Herein, we show that the chemoselectivity of a Zr-MOF/quinone 2 multicatalytic platform can be controlled through modulation of the organic redox co-catalyst. In contrast to previously reported Zr-MOF-808/(hydro)quinone combinations that promote direct oxidation of anilines or thiols, Zr-MOF-808/1,8-dichloroanthraquinone unlocks a different reaction pathway to selectively oxidize primary alcohols in the presence of aromatic diamines and aminothiophenols. This pathway enables the one-pot synthesis of 2-substituted benzimidazoles and benzothiazoles under atmospheric air. Mechanistic experiments support coupled catalytic cycles in which Lewis-acidic Zr sites facilitate quinone-mediated alcohol oxidation, while the MOF/semiquinone interface regenerates the oxidized mediator using oxygen. This method furnishes a highly sustainable synthesis of 31 benzimidazole and benzothiazole products, permitting recovery and reuse of both catalytic components.

item.title: Stoichiometric Control in H2S-Mediated Nitrite Reduction at a Zn-site: Intercepting SNO1−, SSNO1− and HONO Intermediates
item.description: Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) and nitrite participate in intertwined signaling chemistry, yet the factors governing product selectivity between nitric oxide (NO) and nitroxyl (HNO) and the underlying reaction pathways remain poorly defined. Here, we establish that reduction of a zinc-nitrite complex by H2S follows stoichiometry-dependent product selectivity. With 2 equiv of H2S, the reaction generates NO and HNO-derived nitrous oxide (N2O) trapped in 46.3% ± 2.1% and 19.7% ± 1.5%, yields, respectively. UV-vis and 15N NMR spectroscopy along with phosphine-based intermediate trapping and DFT studies support a nucleophilic attack pathway involving zinc-bound thionitrite (SNO−) and perthionitrite (SSNO−) intermediates. We independently synthesize and crystallographically characterize the zinc-perthionitrite complex, identifying isomers with cis-ĸ2-S,O and unprecedented Y-shaped ĸ2-S,S coordination modes in the solid-state. In contrast, 5 equiv of H2S favors an acidbase pathway involving spectroscopically intercepted nitrous acid (HONO) intermediate and affords NO in 94.6% ± 1.5% yield, with only trace N2O. Reaction with hydrosulfide (HS−) instead, generate a zinc-hydrosulfide-nitrite adduct without nitrite reduction; subsequent protonation produces NO exclusively. Together, these findings establish H2S stoichiometry and proton availability as complementary determinants of competing nitrite reduction pathways that control NO versus N2O selectivity at a redox-inactive zinc center.

item.title: De novo Rewriting DNA Identity into Functional RNA via Genetic Information Compiler
item.description: Genetic information is expressed through the molecular products encoded by DNA. Synthetic systems can regulate these outputs, but retain the original link between DNA identity and function. Re-engineering this link could assign new functions to existing DNA identities. Here we present a genetic information compiler (GIC) that converts selected double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) identities into user-defined RNA outputs. GIC exploits the nontrivial activity of λ exonuclease to interrogate dsDNA and release predefined activators. These activators restore T7 promoters and drive programmable transcription. This modular architecture enables orthogonal and concurrent routing, logic processing, and control of RNA identity, amplitude, composition and timing. Spatial compartmentalization further reveals activator-mediated information transfer between separated compartments. By programming functional gRNAs as outputs, GIC enables tunable, sequence-dependent, and selective regulation of Cas9, Cas12a and Cas13a. GIC establishes a new programmable information layer in which existing dsDNA identities can be interpreted de novo as user-defined functional RNAs.

item.title: Topology-Dependent Glass Formation Behavior in Poly[n]catenane Melts with Variable Ring Size and Chain Length
item.description: Poly[n]catenanes consist of cyclic subunits that are connected by mechanical bonds rather than covalent bonds, which gives them internal degrees of freedom and permanent topological constraints that are absent in conventional polymers. How these features affect the glass transition is not known. Here, we employ molecular dynamics simulations of the Kremer–Grest bead–spring model to determine the glass transition temperature, Tg, of poly[n]catenane melts with ring sizes of m = 8–50 beads and chain lengths of n = 5–40 rings. Each melt is compared with a bonded-ring analogue in which the mechanical link between neighboring rings is replaced by a covalent bond. Mechanical interlocking raises Tg by up to 0.44 εkB-1 , nearly a factor of 2, for the smallest rings, whereas the effect vanishes for m ≥ 20. This crossover coincides with the ring size at which the free aperture of a ring, measured in the melt, falls below one bead diameter. The topological contribution to Tg scales as 1 − nend/n with nend ≈ 2.1 for all tightly interlocked chains, indicating that the two singly interlocked terminal rings act as topological chain ends. The Debye–Waller factor, the generalized localization model, and the non-Gaussian parameter show that tight mechanical bonds restrict bead motion at a given temperature, make the relaxation time grow more steeply as the cage tightens, and add a broad, slow, and strongly non-Gaussian component to segmental relaxation. In contrast, the dynamic fragility and the large-scale Gaussian chain statistics are nearly unaffected, and the modest increase of the characteristic ratio cannot account for the rise of Tg. Our work identifies ring size as the primary molecular parameter controlling the glass transition of poly[n]catenanes and shows that it acts through local topological confinement rather than global chain stiffness.

item.title: From MOF to polyMOF: Incorporation of Poly(itaconic acid) into a Cu-Ellagate Framework
item.description: The incorporation of flexible coordinating polymers into crystalline metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) remains challenging because the conformational freedom of macromolecular ligands can interfere with the development of long-range order. Here, we report IEF-35(Cu), a new Cu–ellagate MOF whose crystal structure was resolved by electron diffraction, and its extension to a polymer-containing framework, PolyIEF-35(Cu), through the incorporation of poly(itaconic acid) (PIA) as a co-ligand. The resulting hybrid retained the characteristic features of the parent framework while displaying pronounced changes in particle morphology and gas sorption. Variation of the ellagic acid (EA) to PIA ratio showed that the crystalline hybrid could be obtained over a relatively broad compositional range. Both materials retained their crystallinity upon heating up to 250 °C and exhibited substantial stability toward the investigated solvents. Finally, biological studies showed cytocompatibility under the investigated conditions and antibacterial activity against Staphylococcus epidermidis.

item.title: Unleashing AI for preclinical drug development
item.description: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping preclinical drug development across target discovery, therapeutic design, synthesis, functional characterization and safety assessment. In this review, we present an integrated view of AI across the preclinical pipeline, beginning with target identification, modality selection and representation learning for molecular, protein, structural, cellular and multimodal data. We then examine major generative modeling paradigms including autoregressive, latent-variable, diffusion, flow-based and guided approaches and their applications across small molecules, peptides, enzymes, antibodies, Tcell receptors and mRNA therapeutics. We discuss how these methods support de novo design, structure- and pocket-conditioned generation, sequence–structure co-design, affinity and activity optimization, developability engineering and synthesis-aware discovery. We further review AI-enabled retrosynthesis, reaction prediction and closed-loop experimental optimization, emphasizing the distinction between computational synthesizability and experimentally executable chemistry. Beyond molecular generation, we organize functional prediction from binding and kinetics through target engagement, pharmacological activity, mechanism of action, pathway response and phenotypic outcome. We also examine singlecell perturbation modeling, organoid-based drug-response prediction, toxicity and off-target assessment, and prospective validation across therapeutic modalities. Across these areas, we highlight the importance of uncertainty estimation, out-of-distribution generalization, reproducibility and experimentally grounded benchmarking. Finally, we discuss how integrating generative AI, mechanistic biology and iterative design–make–test–analyze cycles could transform AI from isolated predictive tools into decision-support systems for preclinical drug development.

item.title: Structure-Based Optimization and Biological Evaluation of SARS-CoV-2 3CLpro Covalent Inhibitors
item.description: The global emergence of COVID-19, caused by SARS-CoV-2, has underscored the critical need for effective antivirals against coronaviruses. The 3-chymotrypsin-like protease (3CLpro) of coronavirus has been a primary target for drug development due to its critical role across various coronaviruses. Following our initial report, this study focuses on the structure-based optimization of 3CLpro covalent inhibitors. With the guidance of molecular docking and covalent binding parameters measured from an innovative isothermal titration calorimetry-kinetic competition (ITC-KC) assay, we optimized and synthesized series of potent covalent inhibitors with antiviral activity in cell-based assays.

item.title: FoldX interface ΔΔG depends on which structure it starts from, and a learned predictor does not: a cautionary analysis on glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase
item.description: FoldX and related methods are widely used to interpret missense variants, and their sensitivity to the input structure is documented: repair of the coordinates is mandatory, averaging over structural ensembles improves agreement with experiment, and the uncertainty of a FoldX folding ΔΔG has been put at roughly ±3 kcal/mol, with binding stability worse. What has not been asked is whether that uncertainty is spread evenly over a protein. We took 258 ClinVar missense variants in glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase, a homotetramer, verified every reference residue against the 1SIQ structure and computed ΔΔG for the 124 classified pathogenic. Eighteen variants were then recomputed on three molecular dynamics snapshots of the same complex: six interface variants selected on their monomer-to-tetramer difference, six interface variants drawn at random, and six at least 10 Å from any contact. The displacement between the crystal-based value and the relaxed-frame mean had a median of 1.10, 1.38 and 0.20 kcal/mol in the three groups (random interface against distant, Mann-Whitney p = 0.0130), while frame-to-frame scatter was indistinguishable between them (Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.385). The variation is therefore positional, and it is not explained by noise in the mean. SAAMBE-3D, a learned interface predictor, run on the same eighteen variants and the same four structures, moved by a median of 0.075 kcal/mol at the interface and by nothing at all away from it, so the instability is largely a property of FoldX. It also depends on magnitude: G171R, scored at +22.53 kcal/mol, moved 2.7%, whereas A421V moved from +0.18 kcal/mol, which reads as tolerated, to +4.37 ± 2.22. Along the way we found that ThermoMPNN given a chain selector on a tetramer returns values identical to the isolated monomer at all 7,800 scanned positions. For variant interpretation the consequence is specific: at a subunit interface, in the range where a classification is actually in doubt, a single starting structure does not support a single number.

item.title: From Vacuum Geometry to Solution-Phase Electronic Properties and Thermodynamics via Equivariant Neural Networks
item.description: We introduce a general framework for predicting solution-phase quantum-mechanical (QM) properties of drug-like molecules directly from gas-phase geometries, without solvent-specific structural optimization or property calculations. Using current equivariant neural network (ENN) architectures, such as MACE and Allegro, we demonstrate that they can also predict extensive and intensive QM properties in implicit water at a high level of theory. Direct-and ∆-learning strategies are employed for this prediction task using the Aquamarine dataset, which provides QM properties for the same molecules in both environments. The developed models are systematically evaluated for scalability to larger molecules, transferability across chemical space, and generalization to out-of-equilibrium configurations. Our results show that, despite substantial differences between gas-and solution-phase conformational ensembles, the models can accurately reconstruct ensemble-averaged solution-phase properties from gas-phase molecular dynamics. We further integrate the learned QM properties into the QUEDsol framework (“QUantum Electronic Descriptors in SOLution”) as electronic descriptors for hydration free-energy prediction. A simple and interpretable quadratic regression model trained on the FreeSolv dataset achieves state-of-the-art performance on the challenging and chemically diverse FlexiSol benchmark, outperforming previously reported QM-and ML-based approaches. These results establish ENNs as a versatile approach for inter-phase molecular property prediction and demonstrate that environment-specific QM descriptors generated from gas-phase geometries can provide transferable inputs for complex thermodynamic modeling.

item.title: The Chemical Bond in the Age of Quantum Information: Atoms in Molecules as Entangled Open Systems
item.description: The chemical bond is among the oldest ideas in chemistry and still among the least settled: chemists continue to disagree about what a bond is. We argue that the recurring controversies (ionic versus covalent, dative versus shared-electron, hypervalent versus metavalent, whether metal–metal contacts are genuinely collective) are not disputes about the physics but about an unstated reference against which a bond is declared. Removing the reference forces a change of viewpoint: an atom in a molecule is not a fixed piece of electron density but an open quantum system, a mixed state that is a probabilistic superposition over how many electrons it owns. From this vantage the electronnumber fluctuations that the theory of electron distribution functions has long measured acquire a sharp meaning: they are the quantum correlation, the entanglement, shared between the atoms of a molecule. Measured directly between the Bader basins chemists already draw, this entanglement yields a single, reference-free bond order in which the electron pair of Lewis, the resonance of Pauling and the delocalization of Mulliken reappear not as assumptions but as consequences. We outline the open-systems formulation of Quantum Chemical Topology that makes the picture exact, and sketch how the same quantity is the natural readout of molecular quantum computation.

item.title: A bipartite quantum-acoustic architecture stabilizes multi-exciton solitons at 323 K
item.description: A fundamental thermal paradox has constrained the physical viability of quantum coherent Davydov solitons in protein α-helices for over 50 years. At 323 K (0.0278 eV), ambient thermal noise disrupts the localized amide I self-trapping resonance, rapidly scattering multi-quanta excitations into delocalized thermal states on femtosecond timescales. A non-equilibrium, bipartite quantum-acoustic stabilization matrix resolves this long-standing decoherence gap by inducing a transverse acoustic viscoelastic phonon gap, extending exciton coherence lifetimes from 6.5 fs to 42.6 fs—a pre-thermalization window sufficient to outpace non-radiative dissipation and electrostatically prime catalytic interfaces prior to microsecond motor stepping. Utilizing non-Markovian open quantum system simulations, we demonstrate that a highly polarizable variable-dipole linactant at the lipid raft interface induces localized electrodynamic Stark defects, breaking lattice translation symmetry to anchor the wave packet. Sustaining this protective boundary against passive diffusive loss mandates a strict kinetic equilibrium that arrests uncoupled proton leaks, directly coupling the continuous, hydrogen-bonded α-helices of eukaryotic F/V-type rotary c-rings to a hyper-rigid viscoelastic membrane locked in a far-from-equilibrium state. Finally, we present a definitive pathway to bypass thermal decoherence by establishing three physical boundary conditions to translate these biological principles into a predictive blueprint for synthetic quantum-acoustic metamaterials.

item.title: Gold nanofibers as scaffolds for neuron differentiation in a 3D microtissue
item.description: Engineering neuronal tissues requires biomaterials that provide structural support while actively directing cell fate. Here, high-aspect-ratio gold nanofibers are explored as bioinstructive scaffolds for neuronal organization and differentiation.
