CrIII promotes reduction of these ligands under mild conditions (starting at −0.16 V vs. Fc+/0), providing the first extended material with btpy•− or btpy2− units. Interestingly, (1n+)x undergoes non-integer redox changes (∣Δn∣ < 1) in DMF solution, representing emergent electronic behavior that leads to a moderately high solid-state conductivity of 3.9 x 10−3 S cm−1 when n = 1.5. These solution-phase/solid-state correlations present a promising way to examine and tune the electronic properties of metal-organic radical materials.

item.title: Composition-Dependent Remodeling of the ABCB1Disordered Linker by Plasma-Generated ReactiveMixtures
item.description: Multidrug resistance (MDR) mediated by the efflux transporter ABCB1 (P-glycoprotein) remains a major barrier in cancer chemotherapy. Because classical active-site inhibitors have largely failed clinically due to off-target toxicity, disrupting the interdomain mechanical coupling required for transport has emerged as an attractive alternative. Cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) generates coexisting reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (RONS) capable of sensitizing chemoresistant cells, yet how multicomponent reactive mixtures dynamically perturb the intrinsically disordered NBD1–TMD2 linker, a vital mechanical relay in ABCB1, remains unresolved. Here, we investigate the conformational and mechanical response of the structurally tethered ABCB1 linker exposed to binary and ternary mixtures of H2O2, NO, and O2 using all-atom molecular dynamics simulations. Characterization across a six-descriptor dynamical panel, synthesized into an Integrated Control-Relative Restriction Score (ICRRS), reveals that linker remodeling is governed by chemical composition rather than total molecular loading. Increasing molecular burden does not induce monotonic rigidity; instead, distinct mixture combinations selectively direct the linker toward divergent, polarized states of conformational restriction or conformational release. Crucially, benchmarking against isolated-species counterparts revealed pronounced composition-dependent contrasts, wherein co-solutes redirect local torsional kinetics, spatial breadth, and effective tethered stiffness. These findings establish that coexisting plasma-derived species selectively reconfigure the conformational state of the ABCB1 disordered relay. By demonstrating that mixture biophysics overrides concentration-dependent loading, this work provides an atomistic foundation for how multicomponent plasma biophysics can mechanically modulate ABCB1 allostery, offering new biophysical perspectives for overcoming P-glycoprotein-mediated chemoresistance.

item.title: Memory-Augmented Generative Design of Octahedral Co(II) Complexes with Targeted Zero-Field Splitting
item.description: The discovery of coordination complexes with targeted magnetic anisotropy remains challenging because the enormous chemical space of ligands and coordination environments makes propertydirected molecular design difficult to achieve by conventional screening. Here, we introduce a memoryaugmented generative framework for the inverse design of octahedral Co(II) complexes with targeted zero-field splitting (ZFS). A chemically curated dataset of ~6000 Co(II) complexes, was used to establish a broad electronic-structure landscape spanning positive and negative ZFS regimes. Building on this chemical space, a generative strategy was developed in which ligand structures are iteratively mutated, recombined, and selected according to their predicted magnetic properties, while an elitememory mechanism preserves high-performing molecular motifs and guides subsequent generations toward increasingly favorable candidates. This enables targeted exploration of ligand combinations and coordination environments associated with large negative ZFS while simultaneously controlling rhombicity. The generated complexes were subjected to independent CASSCF calculations, including spin–orbit coupling, to directly validate their magnetic properties. Notably, the generative framework identified candidates with strongly enhanced axial anisotropy, including a representative complex exhibiting D ≈ −223 cm-1 after ab initio validation. The validated candidates reproduced the targeted ZFS with deviations of approximately 15–18 cm-1. These results establish a generative, memory-guided route from ligand design to electronically validated magnetic complexes, providing a practical strategy for discovering previously unexplored Co(II) molecular magnets and advancing molecular-magnet design from screening toward property-directed generation.

item.title: Aerobic ethanol oxidation by magnetic inductive heating of Pd NPs supported onto Ni foam
item.description: Selective aerobic oxidation of ethanol to acetic acid is an attractive example of the conversion of biomass-derived alcohol value-added chemicals. In this context, conventional liquidphase processes often rely on harsh conditions, long reaction times, inefficient external heating and limited catalyst recovery. Herein, a radically new strategy for acetic acid synthesis from ethanol is proposed and demonstrated. The catalyst used is designed not only as the active phase for chemical transformation, but also as the element responsible for local heat generation. Pd nanoparticles were immobilised onto magnetically-responsive Ni foam, affording a macroscopic, flow-compatible architecture that overcomes key limitations found for dispersed or powdered systems, including aggregation, active-phase loss and difficult reuse. Using a low amplitude alternating magnetic field of 9.2 mT, which corresponds to a lower magnetic flux density value than normally used for dispersed magnetic nanocatalyst, the Pd@Ni-foam system reached 90 % ethanol conversion after 8 h, while the acetic acid selectivity was >98 % already after 2 h reaction time. In analogous conditions, conventional heating was significantly less effective than magnetic induction, highlighting the advantage of delivering thermal energy directly at the Pd/liquid interface, thereby preserving ethanol availability at the active sites while limiting substrate evaporation. The structured catalyst showed direct reusability without regeneration, and analysis of the recovered catalyst revealed neither Pd NPs sintering, nor detectable Pd loss. By combining catalytic activity, lowfield magnetic responsiveness, stability, reduced bulk heating and continuous flow operation within a single tuneable material, a new approach to heterogeneous catalysis has been introduced, opening a modular route toward electrified, intensified and more efficient liquidphase transformations of renewable and volatile substrates, such as ethanol.Flow magnetic induction heating reactor with palladium nanoparticles supperted on Ni foamFlow MIH-reactor using a Pd-decorated Ni-foam catalyst for the aerobic oxidation of ethanol to acetic acid. The Ni foam acts as both structured catalyst support and induction-responsive heating element under a low magnetic field of 9.2 mT. The system operates in water and enables high acetic acid selectivity. item.title: A species-resolved well-balanced lattice Boltzmann framework for Maxwell–Stefan diffusion in non-ideal multiphase multicomponent transport
item.description: Simulating non-ideal multiphase multicomponent transport requires coupled solution of phase equilibrium, hydrodynamics, and multicomponent diffusion. Recent thermodynamically consistent and well-balanced lattice Boltzmann formulations have addressed multiphase equilibria, but their integration with multicomponent diffusion is less developed. In this work, a speciesresolved well-balanced lattice Boltzmann framework is developed to incorporate Maxwell–Stefan diffusion into non-ideal multiphase multicomponent transport. The formulation evaluates thermodynamic driving forces from chemical potentials and introduces pairwise interspecies resistance at the species-momentum level while preserving the well-balanced nature of the underlying multiphase model. Asymptotic analysis shows that the species-level force balance reduces to the Maxwell–Stefan constitutive relation under quasi-static diffusive conditions. The framework is assessed by equilibrium and phase separation tests, linear modal benchmarks, Arnold–Toor cross-diffusion cases, local Maxwell–Stefan diagnostics, and a buoyancydriven bubble dissolution illustration. The equilibrium tests recover the theoretical equilibrium compositions with nearly uniform chemical potentials and very low spurious velocities. The modal benchmarks reproduce the predicted exponential decay rates with errors below 0.2% for ideal mixtures and about 0.1–0.5% for non-ideal mixtures, while the Arnold–Toor and local diagnostic tests capture characteristic Maxwell–Stefan diffusion behavior. These results support the proposed framework as a thermodynamically consistent and well-balanced lattice Boltzmann approach for non-ideal multiphase multicomponent transport.

item.title: Pd-catalyzed Cycloadditions of 5-Vinyloxazolidine-2,4-diones: A Diastereo- and Enantioselective Access to Spirooxindoles
item.description: In this manuscript, we report a straightforward route to spirooxindoles by Pd-catalyzed cycloadditions of 5-vinyloxazolidine-2,4-diones with isatins. After a screening of chiral ligands, DTBM-SEGPHOS was selected to induce high diastereo- and enantiocontrol of the two newly created tetrasubstituted stereocenters. Our investigation demonstrated broad functional group tolerance under the reaction conditions. Overall, this work represents a rare example of Pd-catalyzed cycloadditions involving 5- vinyloxazolidine-2,4-diones and electrophilic C=O bonds.

item.title: GMAP: A General Purpose Hamiltonian Mapping Program for Computational Spectroscopy
item.description: Vibrational and electronic spectra provide useful information about structure, dynamics, and function in the condensed phase. Electrostatic mappings have proved to be powerful tools for predicting and interpreting both vibrational and electronic spectra. Numerous special purpose programs exist; however, a general purpose framework is still missing. In this paper, we present a new general purpose mapping program for bridging the gap between structural and dynamical information obtained in molecular dynamics simulations and programs for calculating spectroscopic observables. It comes with a number of preexisting maps to, for example, predict the amide I vibrational spectrum of proteins or to model the electronic Qy band of strongly coupled chlorophyll molecules in photosynthetic systems. The program applying mappings connecting structural or electrostatic properties with excitation frequencies, transition dipoles, and couplings is designed so that the user can easily adapt existing maps or add new maps for desired chromophores.

item.title: Tracking Surface Charge of Gold Single-Crystal Electrodes with Diffuse Layer Force Microscopy
item.description: Electrochemistry is a powerful approach for the interconversion of electrical and chemical energy. This is enabled by the nanoscale confined potential difference occurring at an interface, such as that between a solid and a liquid. As such, the structure of this region of separated charge, or electrical double layer, inherently includes molecular scale ordering in the liquid, as well as atomic scale details of the electrode, making it challenging to obtain a detailed picture of the potential-dependent state of electrochemical interfaces. In this work, we locally measure the long-range electrostatic interaction force (on the order of the screening length) between single-crystal gold electrodes and a microscale probe. Using such force spectroscopy, we observe three distinct electrochemical phenomena through the interaction force, i.e. non-faradaic charging of the interface and the potential of zero free charge, potential-induced surface reconstruction, and electrochemical oxidation of the gold surface. The results are interpreted within the Derjaguin-Landau-Verwey-Overbeek framework, relating the force measurement to the surface charge and the electrochemical state of the interface.

item.title: Aza-Michael Addition of Aliphatic Amines to Weakly Polarised Alkenes via Organobase Catalysis
item.description: The direct addition of aliphatic amines to alkenes offers an atom-economical route to valuable N-alkyl amines, but remains challenging for weakly polarised alkenes. This is because C–N bond formation is poorly driven thermodynamically and difficult to achieve without strongly activating the alkene or generating more reactive nitrogen species. Here we report an organobase-catalysed strategy that enables anti-Markovnikov addition of secondary aliphatic amines to weakly polarised (hetero)aryl alkenes. Kinetic studies and calculations support a mechanism in which the organobase promotes C–N bond formation through hydrogen bonding and noncovalent stabilisation of the addition transition state, followed by rapid deprotonation of the addition complex. The developed conditions were also applicable to challenging C–C bond forming Michael addition reactions with enolate nucleophiles. These findings demonstrate that organobase catalysis can overcome the intrinsic kinetic and thermodynamic challenges associated with closed-shell additions to weakly activated alkenes.

item.title: High-Sensitivity, Dual Ratiometric and Turn-on ABATaRs for Multiplexed Temporal Imaging of Ferroptosis Hallmarks in Living Cells
item.description: We present a computationally-guided workflow for designing dual turn-on and ratiometric Raman sensors. The workflow has been used to rationally design activity-based alkyne tagged Raman, ABATaR, sensors that overcome the inherently low Raman sensitivity via strategic placement of electron-donating and electron-withdrawing groups. An ABATaR sensing scaffold designed via the workflow afforded ~ 9000 times higher Raman scattering cross-section than the dimethylsulfoxide C-H stretching-mode. The sensitivity of the scaffold was compared to that of 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU) to determine Raman intensity versus EdU, RIE, a parameter used to benchmark Raman probes. An RIE value of 170 was obtained which is one of the highest amongst previously reported monoyne and diyne-based Raman probes. The sensitive ABATaR-scaffold was developed into a dual turn-on and ratiometric Fe2+-sensor that was applied to distinctly quantify endogenous cellular labile Fe2+ ion levels. In a key result, live-cell, temporal imaging with the Fe2+-ABATaR sensor revealed that intracellular labile Fe2+ levels progressively increase with ferroptosis while the total Fe-level remains constant. To demonstrate the generalizability of the design workflow, we synthesized an orthogonal ABATaR-sensor for H2O2. The H2O2-sensor was applied together with the Fe2+-sensor along with inherent Raman peaks for cytochromes to enable simultaneous, multiplexed spontaneous Raman imaging of three distinct ferroptosis hallmarks—labile Fe2+, H2O2, and redox-sensitive cytochrome Raman signals—in living cells. Importantly, the ability to pre-design orthogonal ratiometric Raman sensors and simultaneously track three regulators of ferroptosis via discrete non-overlapping Raman peaks highlights the tremendous potential of Raman sensors toward attaining live cell multiplexed imaging and quantification.

item.title: Predicting Water-Induced Demixing of Ionic Liquid Mixtures with Associative Electrolyte PC-SAFT
item.description: Ionic liquids (ILs) can be mixed with other ILs to fine-tune their physicochemical properties. While ILs have been long considered inseparable, recent studies have demonstrated that the controlled addition of water enables the selective recovery of the constituent salts, opening new opportunities for sustainable IL recycling and separation. The rational design of these IL mixtures remains challenging due to the lack of predictive models capable of accurately capturing the interplay between competing short- and long-range interactions in IL-based systems, particularly in multi-IL systems, thereby limiting our ability to guide both the selection of optimal IL components and the development of efficient post-mixing recovery strategies. We propose in this work an associative electrolyte PC-SAFT (aePC-SAFT) model, that incorporates, in a physically balanced manner, the short-range dispersion and hydrogen bonding interactions, as well as the long-range Coulomb interactions. Ion-specific parameters are obtained from homologous series of [CnC1Im][NTf2] (1-alkyl-3-methylimidazolium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide) and [C4C1Im][OAc] (1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium acetate), and subsequently transferred to functionalized ILs, including [C3OC1Im]+ (1-methoxyethyl-3-methylimidazolium), based on the liquid-liquid equilibria (LLE) and density of their mixtures with water and hydrocarbons. Without additional parameter adjustment, the model accurately predicts the LLE of binary and ternary IL-water systems, including the ether-functionalized ILs. This work establishes a robust, predictive, and physically grounded framework for modeling the thermodynamic behavior of ILs, enabling the rational design and optimization of separation processes in IL-based systems.

item.title: Group-aware validation sharply reduces the apparent accuracy of extraction-category classification in public cannabis laboratory data
item.description: Published models that classify cannabis products from cannabinoid and terpene profiles report near-perfect accuracy: above 95% for resin type, 100% for chemovar class. These figures come from random cross-validation or Kennard-Stone partitioning, which hold out no plant, producer or laboratory. We quantify the cost on a task with explicit group structure. On 33,229 public laboratory-result rows for cannabis concentrates that name a producer, nearly all from Nevada, each with a source-declared extraction category (non-solvent against solvent-based), a gradient-boosted classifier scores 78.5% balanced accuracy and a ROC AUC of 0.89 under random five-fold cross-validation. Holding out the producer leaves 54.0% and 0.62. A signal survives: the pooled held-out AUC is 0.61, with a producer-level bootstrap interval of 0.535 to 0.698. But the reported model's pooled balanced accuracy does not separate from chance (51.6%, interval 47.3 to 56.6); it keeps about 30% of its above-chance AUC, and an unweighted logistic regression 41 to 53%. A designed experiment shows the same direction: with the random split averaged over 200 seeds, 162 HPLC-assayed samples fall from 54.3% to 38.9% under leave-one-variety-out with gradient boosting and from 51.8% to 46.3% with logistic regression, against 33.3% chance. In the market data the same profiles identify the producer at 67.1% against a 14.4% baseline and the laboratory at 92.3% against 40.3%. We conclude that the declared extraction category is only weakly recoverable from these analyte panels for an unseen producer, and that a random split overstates it by 8 to 26 points of balanced accuracy depending on the model and subset. We did not rerun the published studies.

item.title: Automated Extraction and FAIRification of Chemical Structures from Scientific Publications
item.description: Chemical structures are published predominantly as images, which makes them inaccessible for database indexing, structure-based search and computational reuse. While Optical Chemical Structure Recognition and PDF-extraction tools attempt post-publication recovery, they cannot restore the information lost during image rendering. To address this, we present BChemXtract, an open-source Java library that extracts chemical structures directly from the CDX and CDXML files that authors already submit with their manuscripts. BChemXtract parses the CDX object hierarchy to isolate chemical fragments from graphical annotations and expands abbreviations using a community-curated lookup table. The structures are then converted via the Chemistry Development Kit into standard machine-readable formats. BChemXtract is integrated into the production workflow of the Beilstein Journals, where extracted structures are manually validated before being embedded in article metadata as Schema.org JSON-LD, deposited in PubChem and offered for download. Applied to the 2993 ChemDraw figures and schemes of volume 20 of the Beilstein Journal of Organic Chemistry, it yielded 23,320 structures with InChIs in under two minutes. On a 225-file benchmark corpus, it generated valid InChIs for 98.2% of extracted unique substances, compared with 14.2% for Open Babel, at comparable per-file speed. BChemXtract makes published chemistry FAIR at the point of publication without altering author workflows. It is available under the MIT license together with a web application and the benchmark corpus.

item.title: Tyr10 Modifications and Peptide Context Rewire GLP-1 Modulation of Amyloid-β42 Assembly
item.description: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) is best known as a receptor agonist, yet its peptide-level behavior in protein-rich environments remains poorly defined. Here, a GLP-1-directed photoaffinity probe recovered a predefined Aβ42 spike-in from cell lysates, while endogenous actin and α-synuclein were detected in the recovered fractions. This observation motivated chemically defined assembly studies with the actinlinked β-thymosin reference TMSB4Y. Thioflavin T (ThT) kinetics and endpoint electron microscopy (EM) revealed no single pro- or antiassembly response. GLP-1 advanced the ThT-positive transition of Tyr10-unmodified Aβ42, whereas TMSB4Y attenuated it. Phosphorylation or nitration at Tyr10 changed both the direction and timing of these effects, and GLP-1 added after assembly had begun redirected established trajectories in a Tyr10-modification-dependent manner. Ser18 O-GlcNAcylation of GLP-1 provided an orthogonal perturbation, suppressing the Tyr10-unmodified response while enhancing the nitrated trajectory and delaying the phosphorylated one. Together, capture in a complex protein background and assembly in defined mixtures identify GLP-1 as a context-sensitive modulator of Aβ42 assembly rather than a fixed promoter or inhibitor.

item.title: Paper2CIF: An AI Agent for Reconstructing Atomistic Models to Discover Structure-Reactivity Relationships
item.description: Reinterpreting published chemical findings requires explicit atomic structures that connect experimental observations with reactivity. Here we report Paper2CIF, an artificial intelligence (AI) agent that reconstructs sample-specific atomic structures from published chemical evidence for structure-reactivity relationship investigations. Across 171 interdisciplinary articles, Paper2CIF achieves 97.08% phase identification accuracy and 91.23% final structural accuracy, with correct structures satisfying all applicable reported constraints, including composition, site occupancy, and local coordination. Calculations on reconstructed BiVO4 structures reveal distortion-dependent spatial contributions to the transition dipole, guiding targeted synthesis toward enhanced near-edge photon conversion. The resulting BiVO4-based Z-scheme pair exhibits a 3.47-fold increase in apparent quantum yield from 4.51% to 15.64% at 475 nm, compared with a 1.03-fold increase from 18.51% to 19.02% at 365 nm. The solar-to-hydrogen efficiency increases from 0.969% to 1.448% for overall water splitting. Paper2CIF establishes atomic reconstruction as a common basis for deriving chemical mechanisms from published evidence and translating them into experimentally testable principles for materials synthesis.

item.title: Metal-Free Photoinduced Divergent Activation of N2O and H2 Employing Main-Group Radical Pairs
item.description: Activating robust small molecules like nitrous oxide (N2O) and molecular hydrogen (H2) without transition metals is a key challenge in sustainable chemistry. To address this, we developed an efficient photochemical platform that uses silylphosphanes to divergently activate both the gases. Under photoirradiation, the silylphosphane’s P-Si bond undergoes rapid homolytic cleavage, releasing highly reactive silyl and phosphinyl radicals. When exposed to N2O, these independent radicals act parallelly to drive a double-deoxygenation cascade, yielding the corresponding tetra-aryldiphosphine dioxide and siloxane. Remarkably, this same transient radical pair can also activate H2 under exceptionally mild conditions. Supported by control experiments and DFT studies that confirm a purely radicaldriven mechanism, this work highlights main-group radical pair as a powerful, sustainable alternative to precious-metal catalysis.

item.title: Unveiling Photoluminescent N-Heterocyclic Silylene-Silver(I) Amides as Dual-Function Photosensitizers and Third-Harmonic Generators
item.description: N-Heterocyclic silylenes (NHSis) have evolved from laboratory curiosities to versatile ligands for small-molecule activation and homogeneous catalysis, yet their potential in photophysics and optical materials remains unexplored. Here, we report for the first time a series of luminescent NHSi-ligated Ag(I) amide complexes (2–4) exhibiting remarkable thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) and dual-emissive behavior. The NHSi→Ag–diphenylamine complex (2) displays pronounced TADF with an exceptionally small singlet–triplet energy gap (ΔES–T ≈ 0.006 eV) and a short delayed-fluorescence lifetime (τTADF ≈ 0.35 μs at 300 K), indicative of efficient reverse intersystem crossing (RISC) driven by NHSi-to-metal amide charge transfer. Complexes 3 and 4 exhibit dual emission and serve as efficient photosensitizers for singlet oxygen (1O2) generation. Remarkably, these complexes (2-4) demonstrate coherent photon up-conversion via third-harmonic generation (THG), representing the first such observation in main-group organometallic chemistry. These findings unveil a new class of main-group metal complexes as promising photosensitizers and third-order nonlinear optical materials.

item.title: From Static Material Design to Predictive Open-Loop Control via Chemistry–Architecture Coupling in a Moving-Boundary Reaction–Diffusion Framework
Hydrogenolysis of N-Cbz-Protected Amines Mediated by Spherical SiliaCat Pd(0)
item.description: The deprotection reaction of N-benzyloxycarbonyl (N-Cbz)-protected amino groups in organic compounds can be efficiently achieved by hydrogenolysis mediated by the sol-gel-entrapped spherical catalyst SiliaCat Pd(0). The heterogeneous catalyst combines high catalytic activity and chemoselectivity with low Pd loading, a nonpyrophoric nature, and excellent reusability. Investigation of the effects of solvent, substrate concentration, Pd loading, temperature, and catalyst particle size revealed that 100 µm spherical SiliaCat Pd(0) provides a favorable balance between rapid reaction kinetics and practical catalyst properties for batch applications. The catalyst was successfully reused over ten consecutive reaction runs, maintaining complete conversion and high isolated yields. A broad substrate scope was demonstrated, with tolerance toward methyl esters, Boc-protected amines, pinacol boronate esters, and an aliphatic bromide, while debromination of an aryl bromide revealed a limitation of the method. Comparison of the 100 µm spherical sol-gel catalyst with several commercial heterogeneous Pd catalysts demonstrates its high catalytic activity and selectivity under mild reaction conditions.

item.title: Mechanochemical nitrogen fixation into amides and nitriles.
Cation Mixing Controls Photocatalytic Activity of Ionic Carbon Nitrides by Switching Exciton Character and Electron Localization
An Annotation Consistency Checker for Evidence-Based Evaluation of Untargeted LC-MS/MS Metabolite Annotations
item.description: Untargeted LC-MS/MS metabolomics routinely produces complex annotation landscapes in which individual spectra can yield multiple candidate metabolite annotations. Although spectral similarity provides an essential foundation for library-based annotation, determining whether a candidate annotation is consistent with the available evidence and whether alternative explanations remain plausible requires integration of multiple lines of evidence. In current practice, this evaluation is largely embedded in expert judgment, making annotation review difficult to teach, standardize, and reproduce. Here, we introduce an annotation consistency checker that aids this expert review process by generating a user-inspectable report for spectral library matches. The framework integrates complementary evidence dimensions, including spectral agreement, structural relationships among candidate annotations, and competing library matches to highlight annotations that are supported by, or inconsistent with, the available data. Biological context is provided separately to aid interpretation of metabolite occurrence across organisms, tissues, and sample types but is not incorporated into the annotation score. By enabling systematic evaluation of multiple evidence streams, this approach provides a transparent workflow that helps users critically assess metabolite annotations, reduce overinterpretation of spectral matches, and make informed decisions beyond only accepting the top-ranked library match.

item.title: Structural Description of Two-Dimensional Nanoscale Networks Using Graph Theory and Graph Growth Algorithms
item.description: Nanostructured networks stand out among other nanostructures for their unique combinations of properties and easily scalable energy-efficient synthesis. Their structural organization is, however, difficult to describe using traditional approaches based on crystallinity. Although revealing distinct structural patterns, the nanoscale networks also have a substantial degree of randomness. Two-dimensional (2D) nanostructured networks self-assembled from nanoparticles present a unique opportunity to develop the methodology for structural description of such materials. We describe nanostructured networks as sets of nodes and edges with corresponding weights taking advantage of the mathematical apparatus of Graph Theory (GT). Being extracted from electron microscopy images, the GT descriptors readily identify nanoscale networks obtained under different chemical conditions. Also important is that among the prior studies the GT description of properties has been extensively discussed, while better understanding of adequate GT descriptors is lagging. All GT descriptors were found to be scale-dependent, with average nodal degree, centrality metrics, multi-fractal dimension, and Ollivier-Ricci curvature following smooth superlinear or sublinear trajectories over several thousands of nodes. Statistical analysis of topological and metric parameters of nodes and edges enables development of topometric graph growth algorithms (TOGGA) that capture the structural uniqueness of each nanoscale network. Similarly to the infinite tiling of unit cells in crystals, TOGGA models enabled the extrapolation of nanoscale network structure, commensurate with both micro- and macroscale samples over 10 million nodes and 20 million edges. The predictions of electric transport through the networks comparable in size to experimental samples enable identification of knowledge gaps for rapid design of conductive nanoscale networks. TOGGA models can be used to map out experimentally realistic structures for inverse design of nanoscale networks.

item.title: An Evidence-Graded Framework for Pharmaceutical Route Selection and Process-Risk Prioritization: A PN6047 Case Study
item.description: Purpose: To develop and demonstrate an evidence-graded framework for screening discovery-scale synthetic routes before experimental process development, using the publicly disclosed route to PN6047, a clinical-stage δ-opioid receptor agonist, as a case study. Methods: No synthesis was performed. Operations exemplified in two patent documents were inventoried; each transformation and its conditions were graded A–D by the strength of public evidence; documented regulatory and hazard attributes were flagged; two process-oriented variants were screened by step count, flags and an evidence-weighted validation burden; and a twelve-item risk register was ranked, with the sensitivity of the prioritization to the author-assigned ratings tested by perturbation. Results: The exemplified route (milligram to gram scale; final N-functionalization isolated in 16% by preparative HPLC) carries 11 documented flags, including an ICH Q3C Class 1 solvent, palladium and a benzotriazole-derived coupling reagent. Variants R1 and R2 carry 3 flags each but a higher validation burden (11 and 15 against 2, linear scale): fewer documented flags did not mean lower development uncertainty. Two risks, impurity purge when crystallization replaces chromatography and the undisclosed route to the vinyl bromide, stayed in the top three in about 87% of perturbations, conditional on the initial risk model. Conclusion: The framework converts public route information into an auditable experimental-prioritization strategy while explicitly separating documented process liabilities from unvalidated alternatives. It does not select a best route; it shows where the evidence is strong or assumed and which experiments carry the highest information value.

item.title: Designing Alloying Interlayers for Metal Anodes in Batteries: Does Nanostructuring Improve Reversibility?
item.description: Metal anodes have been extensively explored as candidates for high-energy rechargeable batteries. However, uncontrolled electrodeposition of metals such as Zn often produces porous, disconnected “dead” metal that limits reversibility. A common mitigation strategy is to introduce an alloying functional layer, which is in general assumed to perform better when nanostructured due to its increased specific surface area and the diffusion scaling relation 𝜏~ 𝐿 2 𝐷 ⁄ . Here, we directly interrogate how the characteristic feature size of an alloying interlayer governs reversibility, using Ag functional layers with building blocks at three representative length scales: 100 nm, a few μm, and 100 μm, approximately. Combining operando visualization with ex-situ structural characterization, we find that Ag layers composed of few-μm particles exhibit the highest Zn plating and stripping reversibility. Coarse, 100-μm Ag particles provide poor areal coverage, such that beneficial Ag–Zn alloying is confined to isolated regions and does not effectively regulate deposition. In contrast, nanostructured Ag reacts rapidly and nearly completely, transforming into bulk intermetallic phases with large volume change that crack and delaminate from the current collector. Few-μm Ag features, on the one hand, provide sufficient surface coverage to promote uniform nucleation; on the other, Ag particles at this few-μm length scale prevent excessive intermetallic conversion and the associated mechanical failure. These results challenge the conventional wisdom that nanostructured layers are inherently more effective and reveal a previously overlooked mesoscopic design window for alloying interlayers. By explicitly linking alloying-layer feature size to diffusion-controlled phase transformation, mesoscale mechanical stability, and electrochemical behavior, this work identifies surface topography as a key design parameter for stabilizing multivalent metal anodes of high-energy batteries.

item.title: Temperature-dependent Hydrocarbon Chain Packing in Fatty Acid Protocell Membranes at Mineral Interfaces
item.description: Fatty acid vesicles generated through water-rock interactions have been proposed as plausible models of protocells on early Earth. However, how mineral surfaces influence membrane properties over a wide range of temperatures remains unclear. Here, we investigate the temperature-dependent phase transition and hydrocarbon chain packing of vesicles composed of decanoic acid (DA) and 1-decanol (DOH) in contact with FeS, a key hydrothermal vent mineral. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed that DOH incorporation enhances orientational ordering of the hydrocarbon chains, forming more densely packed and thermally stable membranes. This enhancement in molecular ordering induced by DOH incorporation was confirmed experimentally by in situ temperature-controlled micro-Raman spectroscopy and cross-polarized optical microscopy. Upon contact with FeS, DA/DOH vesicles preferentially adhered to FeS surfaces and underwent pronounced structural deformation in response to microscale mineral topology. Despite this deformation, the DA/DOH vesicles retained their liquid-crystalline membrane state. These results demonstrate that FeS surface reorganizes hydrocarbon chain packing in fatty acid membranes, suggesting that mineral-associated protocells possess structurally and dynamically distinct membrane states from free-floating vesicles under the thermally dynamic HV environments.

item.title: Multi-fidelity machine learning interatomic potential for the energetics and finite temperature structure of Pt surfaces and nanoparticles
item.description: Accurate accounting of exposed facets and surface sites is central to understanding metal nanoparticle catalysts, but modelling their structure at finite temperatures is computationally expensive. We benchmark the universal interatomic potential UMA (Universal Model for Atoms, Open Catalyst 2020 task) against Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof density functional theory (PBE-DFT) for Pt. UMA underestimates the surface energies of all 13 facets by 11-17 % and the excess energies of 28 differently shaped nanoparticles, each containing less than 500 atoms, most strongly for small particles. We distill UMA into a compact Deep Potential model by pre-training on UMA labelled bulk and slab data, then fine-tune it on a small PBE-DFT dataset that includes nanoparticles. The resulting multi-fidelity machine learning interatomic potential (MF-MLIP) gives a surface-energy root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 2.8 meV Å−2, 21 % lower than a DFT only model trained on the same data. On six nanoparticles, the MF-MLIP improves force accuracy over UMA, reducing the force RMSE by 29-52 %, with the largest gains at surface, edge and vertex atoms. Molecular dynamics at 500 K shows Pt(111) retaining its termination while Pt(100) and Pt(110) change strongly. At 500-700 K, the nanoparticles lose vertex sites and gain edge sites, and some restructure away from their ideal shapes. On the same CPU hardware, the MF-MLIP runs molecular dynamics simulations 60-100 times faster than UMA.

item.title: Coordination-Insertion Copolymerization of Norbornene with α-Olefins using Half-Titanocene Phosphinimide Catalyst
item.description: We previously reported the controlled coordination-insertion polymerization of 2-norbornene (NB) and 5-alkyl-2-norbornenes using a phosphinimide-ligated half-titanocene catalyst (1), affording high-molecular-weight polymers. In this study, the copolymerization of NB with α-olefins, including 1-octene (2), 1-octadecene (3), and 10-undecen-1-ol (4), was investigated to explore the monomer scope and functional group tolerance. Copolymers with Mn values ranging from 2.0 to 20 kg/mol were obtained in moderate to high yields. NB was consumed more rapidly than 2. Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) analysis of the copolymers suggests that an α-olefin-derived titanium alkyl species undergoes chain transfer via a σ-bond metathesis with NB, affording the 2-norbornenyl moiety at the initiating chain end. In addition, copolymers containing up to 7 mol% of 4 were obtained through protecting the hydroxyl group with methylaluminoxane (MAO) prior to polymerization. Collectively, catalyst 1 exhibited broad reactivity, including the coordination-insertion and the σ-bond metathesis reactions, while remaining catalytically active in the presence of the alkoxyaluminum species.

item.title: On the impact of methodological configurations and data variations on chemical recycling life cycle assessment studies
item.description: The comparability of Life Cycle Assessment studies on chemical recycling processes for plastic waste conversion is challenging due to the wide range of investigated feedstocks, datasets, and methodological choices. Thus, this paper investigates the impact of various degrees of freedom within peer-reviewed Life Cycle Assessments of chemical recycling processes on the proposed environmental impact. In detail, methodological degrees of freedom, such as system boundary depth, functional units, allocation methods, and the utilization of substitution credits, as well as data-related degrees of freedom, including the use of plant-level, model-based, literature-derived, or third-party data at different data scales, such as experimental, laboratory, or pilot scale, are considered. Among the investigated Life Cycle Assessment studies, none of them applied the same combination of methodological choices, highlighting the methodological uniqueness of each study. However, changes in either methodological or data-related degrees of freedom substantially affect Life Cycle Assessment results in both magnitude and interpretation: without changing the methodology, data-related degrees of freedom shift the global warming potential for 1 kg of treated waste from 2.5 kg CO2-eq. below that of incineration as the reference waste treatment process to 0.5 kg CO2-eq. above. Utilizing the same database, methodological differences as reported in the investigated studies shift the global The underlined authors contributed equally and share first authorship. warming potential from 2.9 below to 0.3 kg CO2-eq. above the global warming potential of incineration. The same trend is found when comparing the products of chemical recycling to the fossil-based production routes, where the main levers affecting the results were identified as the declaration of products, the handling of side streams, and the choice of energy sources. These findings show that LCA results should not be interpreted on the basis of individual values alone, but in the context of methodological choices, data sources and quality, and sensitivity to both data and methodological assumptions. Without transparency regarding these aspects, reported values are of limited interpretive value and may offer unwanted possibilities for selective interpretation and may ultimately increase the risk of greenwashing in the communication of chemical recycling performance.

item.title: Origin of the Difference between Kohn-Sham and ∆SCF Band gaps for Delocalized Electron–Hole Excitations in Hybrid-Functional Supercell Calculations
item.description: We examine the relationship between ground-state generalized Kohn–Sham (GKS) band gaps and self-consistent ∆SCF excitation energies for delocalized electron–hole excitations in finite periodic supercells. For a vertical excitation at the undistorted ground-state geometry, these two quantities are expected to coincide when the promoted electron and hole remain Bloch-like. This is mostly true with semilocal functionals, but not with hybrid functionals for which the difference increases linearly with the fraction of exact exchange. The origin of this difference is derived from two equivalent viewpoints: the total-energy change associated with the ∆SCF excitation and the occupation-dependent orbital gap shift arising from the self-consistent potential response. The residual energy arises from the orbital-dependent exact-exchange selfenergy associated with the electron-hole pair and decreases approximately as 1/N

item.title: Structure-Activity Relationship Studies of the Complement Regulator-Recruiting Peptide 5C6
item.description: Active recruitment of host complement regulators to biomedical surfaces emerges as a therapeutic strategy to prevent adverse immuno-inflammatory reactions to biomaterials and organ transplants. Coating with the macrocyclic peptide 5C6, which binds and recruits the central complement regulator factor H (FH), was shown to protect clinically relevant surfaces from complement attack. While we previously identified general determinants for the 5C6-FH interaction, more granular structure-activity relationship (SAR) studies have hitherto been missing. In the absence of published target structures, we employed a panel of focused amino acid substitutions combined with biomolecular interaction studies to achieve an SAR profile of 5C6. We identified three positions that are particularly amenable to affinity optimization and combined several changes to produce a next-generation 5C6 analog with enhanced target residence time and serum stability. Biomaterial-related assays suggest that such analogs may confer benefits under stress conditions, providing a path for the further development of 5C6-based coatings.

item.title: Earth-abundant 3d metal-catalyzed enantioselective catalysis towards the functionalization of E/Zalkenes mixtures.
item.description: Enantioselective catalysis transforming alkenes to chiral molecules have been a breakthrough in the field of organic synthesis. Though a major challenge persists. The “privileged” chiral catalyst capacities depend on the geometry of the olefin substrate which can be either E or Z. Enantioselective catalysis allowing to convert both alkene stereoisomers to a single chiral molecule promises sustainable synthetic routes and novel mechanistic strategies towards chiral molecule synthesis. Enantioselective methods towards the functionalization of E/Z-alkenes, which has largely taken advantages of the recent development of earth-abundant 3d metal catalysis, are covered in this revue. An emphasis on the mechanisms accounting for the observed stereoconvergence and enantioselectivity is proposed.

item.title: Multinotch Isolation Enables Efficient Native Top-down Mass Spectrometry of Proteins in Complex Mixtures.
item.description: Accurate identification of intact proteoforms and their complexes directly from heterogenous biological samples is essential to understand their role in health and disease. While native top-down mass spectrometry (nTDMS) workflows enable this, the extreme molecular complexity of biological samples inadvertently results in overlapping signals which confounds protein identification. One approach to resolving this complexity is gas-phase ion-ion reactions which separate analytical targets according to their original charge state. Charge reduction techniques coupled to mass spectrometry resolve signal overlap in m/z space, when ions differ in charge, and so they are especially useful in the analysis of large biomolecules like proteins that form multiple charge states during electrospray ionisation. Previously, we investigated multistage nTDMS of intact proteins sampled directly from tissue sections where the first experiment stage was separation by charge reduction, followed by collisional activation for sequence ion production. The specificity of product ion spectra was improved but at the expense of signal intensity owing to inefficient use of charge-reduced product ions. Here we establish the use of synchronous precursor selection (SPS) for nTDMS via multinotch isolation in a linear ion trap, enabling simultaneous isolation of multiple targets in m/z space and thereby increasing the number of ions available for fragmentation. We implemented SPS for nTDMS across three charge reduction techniques and collision, electron and photon mediated fragmentation methods on commercial and modified mass spectrometers. Improvements to the signal-to-noise ratio of product ions resulted in greater sequence coverage for example intact proteins and complexes up to ~44 kDa using the SPS workflow. We provide a freely-available SPS target calculator, Novalap, that enables simple SPS method development. SPS nTDMS is a methodological breakthrough for proteoform identification in complex mixtures, where specificity is essential, sequence coverage is desired and ion abundance is at a premium.

item.title: Designing organic photoredox catalysts as a fragment-based puzzle solved by reinforcement learning
item.description: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a promising strategy for identifying optimal solutions in vast search spaces. We have developed a framework in which the design of organic photoredox catalysts (OPCs) is deliberately formulated as a fragment-based puzzle that is well suited to RL. In this framework, an RL agent sequentially selects and orders molecular fragments and attempts to identify fragment combinations that afford high rewards, as calculated based on the similarity between the properties of the generated molecules and those of 4CzIPN, a well-known OPC. In addition to the rediscovery of a previously reported high-performance OPC, experimental validation of the proposed candidates revealed a TADF emitter with redox potentials similar to those of 4CzIPN, as well as an OPC with superior catalytic activity in several photoreactions.

item.title: Probing Benzoxazine Dimer Formation Using Methyl-Blocked Derivatives as Mechanistic Probes
item.description: The early-stage dimer formation of 1,3-benzoxazine (PH-a) was investigated as a diagnostic system for understanding the ring-opening polymerization (ROP) mechanism using a coupled FAIMS-IRMPD-MS/MS platform. High-field asymmetric waveform ion mobility spectrometry (FAIMS) resolved the protonated PH-a dimer into three distinct populations. A series of methyl-blocked benzoxazine derivatives was used to systematically eliminate individual reactive sites and assign each FAIMS population to a specific reaction route via tandem MS fragmentation patterns and IRMPD action spectroscopy, supported by theoretical vibrational spectra obtained by DFT calculations. Four dimer formation pathways were confirmed: phenolic aromatic substitution at the ortho and para positions, and arylamine aromatic substitution at the ortho and para positions of the aniline ring. Phenoxy- and nitrogen-mediated attack routes were not observed. Each pathway yields dimers in either a closed-ring (CRB) or open-ring (ROP) form, a structural duality with direct implications for the crosslinking topology and network heterogeneity of the resulting polybenzoxazine.

item.title: Birefringence Breaks Symmetry-Protected Fluorescence Trapping in Laser-Cooled Crystals
item.description: Total internal reflection traps light inside high-index emitters, and in laser-cooled crystals the trapped fluorescence limits how far purification lowers the parasitic heat load. The symmetry of the crystal shape is known to govern this trapping. Here we show that the dielectric tensor supplies a second, intrinsic symmetry, and we unify the geometric and dielectric symmetries in a single conservation law. A fluorescence photon stays trapped when every facet operation conserves a wave-vector component that keeps it inside total internal reflection. Mirror facets of a cuboid conserve three components and trap 17.2% of all directions. Brewster end facets, or mode conversion between ordinary and extraordinary waves at facets containing the optic axis of uniaxial Yb:YLF, leave one component and reduce the trapped set to a universal shell of 3.45% of directions. Sub-degree misorientation of the optic axis, subnanometer facet roughness or an asymmetric cut releases this shell, and the release rate determines how strongly purification lowers parasitic loss. Released Yb:YLF crystals keep nearly linear purity leverage at 77 K and tolerate about ten times more cold background and up to 240 times more facet absorption than the same crystals with mode-conserving reflection. Birefringence releases trapped light on the smoothest facets, where surface absorption is lowest. item.title: Optimization of Sodium-Catalyzed Si–N Bond Formation Through a Comparative Study of Group 1 Alkoxides
item.description: A systematic comparison of group 1 tert-amylate (OtAmyl) salts as precatalysts for Si–N heterodehydrocoupling is reported with a focus on NatOAmyl. The heavier alkali metals provide good to excellent conversions with all substrates screened, including tertiary silanes and secondary amines, which are challenging substrates in prior literature reports. Although the activity of NatOAmyl is limited in comparison to rubidium and cesium congeners, this can be improved with judicious solvent choice, particularly DMSO. The overall findings support that a single inexpensive and sustainable catalyst can be primarily used for Si–N bond formation; however, if the substrates are particularly challenging, CstOAmyl will provide high conversion. This analysis provides a systematic approach for pragmatic catalysts to engage in bond formation with abundant silicon and nitrogen that serves synthesis and materials chemistry.

item.title: QMzyme: A Python Package for Automated and Systematic QM-based Enzyme Modeling
item.description: We introduce QMzyme, a Python package to automate the generation of Quantum mechanics (QM)-based enzyme models. QM calculations on enzymes are computationally challenging because full enzyme systems typically contain thousands of atoms, placing accurate QM treatments beyond practical computational limits.Therefore, QM-based enzyme studies rely on identifying a subset of atoms that captures the essential chemistry of the reaction environment, enabling tractable yet chemically meaningful calculations. However, constructing these reduced models requires numerous user-defined decisions, including selection of the starting structure, identification of atoms to include in the QM region, and definition of truncation strategies for QM-only models, all of which can substantially influence the resulting calculations. QMzyme aims to provide the community with a flexible and extensible framework for automated, systematic generation of QM-based enzyme models, enabling researchers to more rigorously evaluate how model construction decisions influence computational outcomes while improving reproducibility and transparency across workflows. By facilitating high-throughput generation and analysis of QM enzyme models, QMzyme supports largescale, data-driven investigations of enzyme structure, function, and reactivity. This effort is especially crucial for the creation of large, chemically consistent datasets that can support emergent artificial intelligence and machine learning approaches for accelerated digital discovery in enzymology and biocatalysis.

item.title: Total Synthesis of Site-Specifically Modified bHLHLz Transcription Factors Reveals Insights into the Regulatory Role of Posttranslational Modifications in the Myc–Max–Mad Network
item.description: The Myc–Max–Mad bHLHLz transcription factor (TF) network regulates the expression of ~15% of the human genome, and its dysregulation is implicated in nearly 70% of human cancers. Although its activity is primarily governed by competition for dimerization partners and occupancy of shared DNA target sequences, the molecular mechanisms controlling oligomerization and DNA binding remain elusive. Here, we employed total protein synthesis and combinatorial assembly to define how posttranslational modification (PTM) patterns regulate the Myc–Max–Mad TF network. Using native chemical ligation, we prepared a library of site-specifically modified Myc, Mnt, Mad, and phosphorylated or acetylated Max analogs. Remarkably, the isolation of homogeneous TFs enabled the combinatorial generation of all 24 heterodimeric complexes, allowing systematic analysis of dimerization and DNA-binding activity across the network. Our findings provide direct evidence that although Max phosphorylation and acetylation do not significantly affect its oligomerization with the Myc transcriptional activator, these modifications enhance its dimerization with the transcriptional repressors Mnt and Mad. Moreover, we found that Max-PTMs modulate DNA-binding activity by both specific PTM patterns and combinations, as well as the identity of the TF partner. Together, these findings demonstrate that PTM-dependent modulation of DNA-binding activity within the Myc–Max–Mad network constitutes a key regulatory layer governing gene expression.

item.title: Structural Convergence of MD simulations on RNA Motifs: A tRNA case study
item.description: A detailed understanding of the structural dynamics of diverse RNA architectures is critical for elucidating the chemical basis of cellular function and expanding the use of RNA in medicine and biotechnology. While classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can provide this much-needed atomic information, sampling requirements remain poorly characterized for RNA systems. In the present study, we compared the conformational ensemble sampled by five independent 5 μs trajectories and 60 independent 500 ns replicas for unmodified Escherichia coli tRNAPhe under three (monovalent, crystallographic-Mg2+, and 6 Mg2+) environmental conditions, yielding 165 μs of aggregate sampling. Although the global L-shaped tRNA fold was retained across all simulations, structural convergence was strongly motif-dependent. Mean base-pair and base-step descriptors of the rigid acceptor and anticodon stem-loop duplex regions were reproduced with modest replication across metal environments. In contrast, the dynamic anticodon loop exhibited substantial trajectory-to-trajectory heterogeneity. A stacking-based analysis identified diverse loop conformations with counterparts in experimentally determined tRNA structures, showing that ensembles of independent classical MD replicas can sample diverse experimentally observed conformations without enhanced sampling. While fewer long trajectories incompletely sampled the heterogeneous loop conformational space, ensembles of many shorter replicas are key to exploring the conformational dynamics of RNA motifs like hairpins. Inclusion of Mg2+ also shifted the sampled conformational ensemble, underscoring the importance of mimicking the experimentally-relevant ionic environment. Overall, our findings offer practical guidelines for MD simulation setup, including trajectory length, replica number, and divalent ion conditions, for studies of RNA systems featuring similar tertiary architectures.

item.title: Alkyl-BODIPYs as a Self-Photoredox Catalyst for their Oxidative Hydroxymethylation
item.description: The adoption of photocatalytic approaches for utilising small organic molecules in self‑catalysed reactions offers opportunities in green organic synthesis. We report that alkylated boron‑dipyrromethenes (BODIPYs) act as self‑photoredox catalysts for their own oxidation under mild visible‑light conditions. Using an imidazolinium salt (NHC-H) as a quencher, alkylated BODIPYs are oxidised cleanly to the corresponding hydroxymethyl derivatives in a one‑pot process. Luminescence studies, including Stern–Volmer analysis, support a reductive‑quenching pathway in which the NHC-H transfers an electron to photoexcited BODIPY to give a BODIPY radical anion. The method proceeds without external photocatalysts or stoichiometric oxidants and shows good functional‑group tolerance, highlighting the potential of these chromophores both as substrates and catalytic light absorbers. Moreover, the synthesized molecules were demonstrated to behave as effective passivating agents for layered Mn2+

item.title: Chemically modified hydrogels to improve geothermal reservoir performance by enabling flow control via size-shifting microspheres
item.description: Thermal short circuits, where fluids preferentially connect injection and production wells, are a leading cause of premature enthalpy decline in geothermal reservoirs. These pathways accelerate cooling, reduce effective heat transfer area, and limit reservoir lifetime. We propose a temperature-responsive hydrogel microsphere suspension as an “active tracer” that dynamically redirects flow away from cooled short-circuit channels while also tracing fluid flow via fluorescence spectroscopy. Highly idealized reservoir simulations with field-informed permeability distributions indicate that a yieldstress fluid with temperature-responsive behaviors may improve reservoir thermal lifetime by a factor of at least 24 to 59x while maintaining acceptable hydraulic performance. To develop a candidate “active” tracer intended to satisfy the assumptions of the idealized simulations, we synthesized poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (pNIPA) microgels, characterized their swelling and rheological behavior, and conducted a large-scale laboratory experiment in an analog parallel-plate that demonstrates short-circuited flow behavior. These lab-scale results demonstrate that injected microgels clog cooled short circuits via swelling and diverted flow into hotter regions. This proof-of-concept establishes an attractive pathway for employing engineered materials to actively manage flow and extend geothermal reservoir lifetimes.

item.title: VISION-BASED DRY-MATERIAL INVENTORY ESTIMATION IN AUTONOMOUS LABORATORIES: RGB SEGMENTATION VERSUS RGB-D SURFACE RECONSTRUCTION
item.description: Reliable dry-material inventory monitoring is needed for autonomous laboratory operation, but the suitability of a non-contact method depends on material behaviour, optical access, calibration requirements and the quantity to be estimated. We compared two vision-based approaches—material-specific RGB/YOLO level estimation and visible-surface reconstruction from an Intel RealSense D405—across three materials (black polypropylene pellets, wood powder, and microcrystalline cellulose fine powder) in small transparent laboratory tubes representative of common dosing instruments, with the aim of informing a practical, evidence-based framework for choosing between such methods in laboratory automation and similar industrial contexts. Software-coordinated records linked the two camera channels to a nominal mass-fraction inventory reference and a manual-height baseline. Across six runs and 133 paired, reference-eligible material states, D405 achieved lower error than YOLO in every run (mean absolute error of 3.26 vs. 7.14 percentage points), though YOLO offered higher valid-result coverage (97.2% vs. 95.1%). Both methods showed increased error under repeated surface disturbance, with YOLO degrading more sharply than D405. An exploratory correction fitted using the first observation at each mass level substantially improved YOLO but did not surpass D405’s uncorrected accuracy, while a single global correction worsened both methods—indicating that simple corrections do not transfer robustly across conditions. The results support a method-selection framework based on error, availability, viewing geometry, calibration-state representativeness and total resource requirements. Conclusions are limited to the tested materials and setups, and the mass-fraction reference is an operational inventory proxy rather than a direct measurement of true occupied volume.

item.title: Predictive Model for Acid-Catalyzed SN1 Solvolysis Racemization of Chiral Alcohols in Water
item.description: We have developed a predictive model for assessing the racemization risk of drug candidates featuring chiral alcohol motifs, addressing an important concern in drug discovery and development. Specifically, it predicts the activation free energy of stereoisomerization through the acid-catalyzed SN1 solvolysis mechanism based on the calculated electronic reaction energy associated with carbocation formation, the assumed rate-determining step. At the core of the framework is a linear regression model relating the calculated electronic reaction energy difference between the chiral alcohol and the carbocation intermediate to the activation free energy derived from experimental racemization kinetics. The resulting model showed a strong correlation and high statistical significance (R2=0.92, p=1.9 ∗ 10−8), reproducing the activation free energy with a root-mean-square error of 4.1 kJ/mol. Thus, the model has the potential to enable high-throughput assessment of racemization risk in drug candidates, supporting the development of safer pharmaceuticals and more efficient drug development pipelines.

item.title: Probing Oxygen Transport in β-Cyclodextrin–Cyclohexane Crystal Nanochannels by Luminescence Quenching from Nanoseconds to Seconds
item.description: Molecular transport in nanochannels can deviate from normal diffusion and exhibit different regimes depending on the observation timescale. However, resolving them from nanoseconds to seconds remains challenging. Here, oxygen transport in β-cyclodextrin–cyclohexane supramolecular crystals containing solvent-filled nanochannels is probed using room-temperature phosphorescence and fluorescence of aromatic luminophores. Their emission lifetimes, ranging from approximately 50 ns to 15 s, provide intrinsic time windows spanning more than eight orders of magnitude. Comparison of fluorescence and phosphorescence quenching for the same guests provides an internal control for probe identity. The effective bimolecular quenching rate constants decrease by approximately five orders of magnitude. Between approximately 50 ns and 10 ms, the dependence follows a power law, kq ∝ τ0-0.8, followed by a nearly lifetime-independent plateau. The theory of diffusion-controlled reactions relates this dependence to the time-dependent oxygen flux and indicates subdiffusive transport at intermediate times with an effective anomalous exponent of approximately 0.4. A random-barrier model with quenched disorder provides a physical interpretation of this regime and its crossover to normal transport at long times. Thus, molecular excited states with different emission lifetimes enable luminescence quenching to resolve distinct temporal regimes of molecular transport under nanoscale confinement.

item.title: A Redox-Non-Innocent Catecholate Shifts the Oxidation State Break in the Actinides
item.description: Realizing the full potential of actinide-based systems requires strategies to differentiate elements whose similar chemical properties complicate their selective use. Redox-active ligands offer a promising approach: their ability to participate in electron transfer provides a means to tune the oxidation states and electronic structures of both lanthanides and actinides. To explore this approach, we conducted a theory-guided study of (Tp*)2An(dtbsq) complexes (1-An; An = U, Np, Pu, Am, Bk; Tp* = [HB(C3N2Me2H)3]-; dtbsq•− = [C6O2 tBu2H2]-), which contain a redox-active semiquinone ligand. This study reveals a shift in the preferred actinide oxidation state from An(IV) to An(III) between the chemically similar elements Np and Pu. Such an effect is made possible due to differential stabilization of oxidation states by the ligated redox-active ligand. Structural and spectroscopic data are consistent with this trend, as exemplified by the experimentally characterized complexes 2-U ([(Tp*)(Bp*)UIV 2(dtbc)3], Bp* = [H2B(C3N2Me2H)2]-, dtbc = [C6O2 tBu2H2]2-) and 1-Pu [(Tp*)2PuIII(dtbsq)]. In these systems, the radical ligand is reduced to a catecholate only in the presence of UIII but it remains in its radical form with PuIII. Electronicstructure calculations for (Tp*)2An(dtbsq) (An = U, Np, Pu, Am, Bk) reveal tunable AnIII/IV oxidation states—supported by highly multiconfigurational ground states—and oxidation-statedependent covalency. This study advances our fundamental understanding of actinide bonding and highlights oxidation-state control as a promising strategy for tuning reactivity and selectivity across f-block chemistry.

item.title: Bio-derived ionic conductive Guar Gum hydrogels as distributed circuit elements for analogue signal processing: the case of Resistor-Capacitor filters
item.description: Developing functional electronic materials from renewable resources is a key challenge toward more sustainable electronics. Here, we report on a bio-derived ionic conductive hydrogel based on guar gum and demonstrate its direct integration as a functional circuit element for analogue signal processing. Ionic conductivity is introduced by incorporating sodium chloride into the polysaccharide matrix and systematically tuned through the glycerol and salt contents. Increasing glycerol loading enhances conductivity, while varying NaCl concentration produces a non-monotonic response, with maximum conductivities in the 10-2 S cm-1 range and an optimum salt-loading window. The conductive formulation is subsequently combined with pristine guar gum, used as a dielectric, to fabricate guar gum-based resistor-capacitor elements. Their integration into low-pass and high-pass filters demonstrates frequency-selective operation in the audio range, with cut-off frequencies of 658 and 576 Hz and transition slopes of −17 and +15 dB dec-1, respectively. These results demonstrate that guar gumbased ionic hydrogels can move beyond conventional roles as substrates or electrolytes and directly perform circuit-level functions, providing a simple materials platform for low-frequency analogue electronics.
